title: Supreme Court Allows New Hampshire To Bar Student IDs At Polls For Midterms
desc:
Supreme Court Allows New Hampshire To Bar Student IDs At Polls For Midterms

Authored by Matthew Vadum via The Epoch Times,

The Supreme Court sided with New Hampshire Republicans, allowing officials to stop accepting student ID cards as valid proof of identity for voting.

The high court cited the Purcell principle, which guards against changes to election rules close to Election Day.

The court's decision took the form of an unsigned opinion issued late on Oct. 22.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

The Supreme Court here applied the so-called Purcell principle against last-minute judicially ordered changes to election rules.

A state law known as HB 323 forbids the use of student IDs as valid proof of identity when voting. New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan issued guidance directing election clerks not to accept student IDs as a backup form of identification.

A group called the Coalition for Open Democracy challenged both the state law and the directive in federal court. The group's attorneys argued that the law ran afoul of both the U.S. and New Hampshire constitutions and discriminated against young voters on the basis of age. They also argued Scanlan exceeded his lawful powers as secretary of state.

Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante denied the group's request to bar enforcement of HB 323, but temporarily blocked Scanlan from advising election clerks that student IDs were never acceptable. Days later, the judge extended his order to cover public statements to that effect made by Scanlan. Together, the two orders meant clerks had to keep treating a student ID card as possible backup proof.

In its emergency application to the Supreme Court, the state argued that the district court's order came a mere 32 days before the general election, and that this goes against the Supreme Court's rulings, which have repeatedly held that lower federal courts should not "intervene in state election procedures in the lead up to an election."

The justices stayed Laplante's orders.

"This Court has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election," the justices wrote, citing a 2020 precedent. "Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle."

In her dissent, Jackson said Laplante had determined that it was necessary to correct Scanlan's "publicized misstatement about what New Hampshire's election rules require."

The injunction issued by the district court, Jackson said, "was reasonably designed to address alleged misinformation, not to change the law."

"An injunction to prohibit that conduct does not contribute to public confusion, it prevents that very problem," she said. "I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State's electoral processes."

New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella hailed the Supreme Court's ruling.

"New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written," he said in a statement.

"The Supreme Court's decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials."

The Coalition for Open Democracy criticized the high court's new ruling, calling it "wrong" and a misinterpretation of the Purcell principle.

"We applaud Justice Jackson for her dissent, in which she stands for the Constitution, the right to vote, and a rational application of Purcell," the group said in a statement.

"We will continue to vigorously litigate this case in the defense of the fundamental right to vote of young voters across New Hampshire."

The Supreme Court's order remains in effect through the Nov. 3 general election, while the case continues on appeal in the lower courts.

title: France Braces For Moody's Downgrade As OAT-Bund Spread Hits EU Crisis Level Highs
desc:
France Braces For Moody's Downgrade As OAT-Bund Spread Hits EU Crisis Level Highs

France faces a potential credit rating downgrade later today as social unrest, a deteriorating welfare state, a deficit crisis, political paralysis, and years of uncontrolled mass migration collide, forcing the government to repair its finances or risk sparking the next Eurozone crisis.

UniCredit fixed-income strategist Francesco Maria Di Bella told clients earlier, "Tonight, Moody's will review France's credit rating, which is currently at Aa3 with a negative outlook."

Di Bella outlined his expectations for Moody's upcoming ratings decision:

We expect the rating agency to downgrade French public debt as deteriorating fiscal indicators are compounded by political constraints that hinder efforts to place public finances on a more sustainable path.

With S&P and Fitch already placing the country's rating credit one notch lower, we think this move is broadly expected and should not lead to a further underperformance of French govies.

The 10Y OAT-Bund spread is currently trading at around 175bp, 90bp wider than at the beginning of September and at the highest level since its peak in November 2011.

That said, a rating downgrade would keep investor attention high on the political uncertainty and weakening economic fundamentals in France.

Next year's presidential election represents a source of concern not only for France but for the entire eurozone, and adds to other risk factors such as geopolitical tensions and elevated energy prices.

Bank of America co-head of global rates strategy Sphia Salim wrote in a note:

Attention is firmly on risk assets. The equity sell-off, wider credit spreads and OAT-Bund breakout increasingly reinforce one another, adding momentum to the duration rally alongside the continued short covering by CTAs & bid for receivers.

After close, we will also get Moody's rating decision for France. If Moody's doesn't deliver a downgrade and simply reaffirms the negative outlook, the decision could offer some reprieve to OAT-Bunds. Absent a stabilization in spread, the pressure will be on the ECB to deliver at least some verbal intervention (Rates - EU).

France's OAT-Bund spread widened to 175 bps Friday morning, approaching levels seen at the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis.

France's CDS spreads suggest investors are pricing its sovereign risk more like a low single-A or high-BBB credit.

Here's more commentary from Cosimo Codacci-Pisanelli and Rikin Shah via Goldman Sachs:

PRESSURE ON FRANCE BUILDS...

10y OAT-Bund closed at 173bp on Thursday, the widest since November 2011, and France now trades 45bp through Italy. The forced deleveraging of two weeks ago has stopped, yet spreads have gone well through the 12-Oct highs anyway. This is a fundamentals story, not just a positioning one.

Last weekend's protests were the largest since the yellow vests and the 2019/2023 pension strikes, and a post-protest poll now puts Melenchon in the second round. The direct growth hit from the riots looks small, but it is another headwind to an already weak growth outlook: GIR have downside risks to their 2027 growth forecast 0.6% vs the government's 1.0%. Even in the constructive scenario, where the 5.0% 2027 budget deficit target passes by year-end, GIR expect the deficit to realise at 5.3% given their weaker growth forecast. The arithmetic is challenging and unforgiving. With an assumption of 1% real growth, 2% inflation and a 4% borrowing cost, stabilising the debt needs a primary surplus of ~1%, something France has rarely come close to (chart). If funding costs converge to where 10y OATs trade today, just above 5%, that requirement drifts towards 2%. The bigger takeaway from the protests is that this is not a society ready to accept that scale of adjustment, whatever the political will.

There is undoubtedly a market structure component to the moves too. Positioning in the front end has been reduced and changed hands at better levels in the recent sell-off, but is still long. Further out the curve, the most striking thing has been the lack of buying.. even fair value models screening OATs as ~60bp cheap, value alone hasn't brought real money in. So what turns buying momentum? An energy-relief-driven duration rally might help, as might lower vol. Really it needs some fundamental improvement in the outlook... and in the short term that looks challenging, with the calendar showing more potential headwinds than tailwinds: Moody's review today, more protests expected this weekend, downside risks to Q3 GDP (first print 30 Oct), strikes expected on 5th Nov and a the Melenchon rally on 6th Nov. It's hard right now to see a material trigger for a material reversal in spreads, with further widening at risk of becoming even more convex from here. The risk of such moves ahead of clear event risk is enough to deter fair value buyers for now.

France's lower house scrapped key savings measures from the 2027 budget this week, undermining efforts to bring the deficit down to 5% of GDP from 5.4% this year. Opposition parties have shown no appetite for compromise ahead of the presidential election, rejecting spending cuts while pushing for additional outlays.

"You want to wait and see how the narrative evolves over the next six months into the election. That's going to have a more meaningful impact on the spread," said Rushabh Amin, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments.

Mike Bell of RBC BlueBay Asset Management expects it could get even uglier if Moody's, S&P, and Fitch all lower France's rating into the BBB category, the lowest investment-grade tier.

title: Dolly Parton's Sister Says Tennessee Machine Kept Defaulting To Blackburn; State Claims "Not A Vote Flipping Situation"
desc:
Dolly Parton's Sister Says Tennessee Machine Kept Defaulting To Blackburn; State Claims "Not A Vote Flipping Situation"

Stella Parton, Dolly Parton's younger sister, says a voting machine at the Hermitage Library in Davidson County kept selecting Republican gubernatorial nominee Marsha Blackburn, a candidate she says she would never vote for, forcing her to correct her ballot three times. Mediaite flagged her post. Tennessee's elections coordinator calls such reports unintended touches, and says the paper ballot, not the screen, is what gets counted.

"In Tennessee last week at the Hermitage Library where I voted, I had to go back three times and correct my vote because it kept defaulting to Marsha Blackburn," Parton wrote on Facebook. "Don't let them rig this election." Blackburn, a sitting U.S. senator, faces Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilmember, in the governor's race.

Parton said she finally called over a poll worker on the third try, and she urged voters to "double check your ballot before you print it out and put it through the machine." It's unclear whether the problem was a malfunction, user error or something else.

She is not the only one. WSMV reported on Oct. 20 that Jackie Herrud, who voted at the Longview Recreation Center in Spring Hill in neighboring Williamson County, said, "I kept punching for the Democrat, Jerri Green, and it kept punching back to Marsha Blackburn." Poll workers there told her they had heard similar complaints. Another Williamson County voter, Toni Fitzgerald, said the button was hard to press and she kept pressing until it registered; her site had no stylus.

In response, Tennessee's Secretary of State's office said it had received one matching complaint out of about 400,000 voters as of that Oct. 20 report, and pointed to the selection screen, the review screen and the paper record as safeguards. More calls came in after the story aired.

By the next day, Elections Coordinator Mark Goins told WSMV: "It's not a vote flipping situation. It's normally like an unintended touch that they may not even realize." He added, "In all the situations, since I've been here, that's exactly what's occurred." Goins said the marking device stores no votes, and the paper ballot is what gets counted. "They're actually being counted on that paper ballot that's going in the scanner," he said. WSMV reported that Davidson and Williamson counties use ballot marking machines, while other counties use different equipment.

For each reported problem, Goins said, his office contacts the county and sends one Republican and one Democratic technician to examine the machine. Neither WSMV report describes the results of any such inspection.

Davidson County Elections Administrator John Richardson told WSMV that about 65,000 people had voted early in the county and only a few had called with concerns. The county is bringing back stir sticks, which work as styluses, because "when they use their finger it doesn't necessarily connect." It used them in 2024 and dropped them over plastic-use concerns. Richardson told NewsChannel 5 the touchscreens, in use for about a decade, respond to pressure, so fingers or nails can be less precise. A Davidson County voter there, Gladys McCowen, said she pressed the middle of Jerri Green's name and Blackburn's appeared, but her paper ballot was accurate. Blackburn urged voters to report irregularities to their local election commission, and Green's campaign manager said voters had reported switching away from Green.

Tennessee has been here before. At an Aug. 5 press conference held jointly by Shelby County's Democratic and Republican parties and the Memphis NAACP, NAACP member Gale Jones Carson said a machine selected a different candidate than the one she chose, and that it took three tries. Separately, the county election commission blamed "human error" for one early voting machine in Bartlett that omitted four state judicial races for 307 voters. In 2024, Shelby County officials said they found no irregularities after similar claims, and in Texas, Tarrant County said one of 58,000 first-day ballots was misprinted due to voter error, CBS News reported at the time.

** PRESS RELEASE ** pic.twitter.com/YC5Gazwnet

— Tarrant County Elections (@tarrantelection) October 22, 2024

Calibration is the likeliest technical explanation on offer. An election expert told the Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington there are known calibration issues with some older touchscreens, including some used in Tennessee. No cause has been established for any of the Tennessee reports, and no independent inspection of the machines has been published.

Mediaite also cited Nashville turnout "15 times higher" than the 2022 midterm. WPLN reported that figure compares first-day in-person voting, up about 1,400% from 607 voters at the city's sole polling site in 2022. With mail ballots the increase is about 240%, and against the 2018 governor's race, first-day turnout fell nearly 20%. Early voting runs through Oct. 29, and Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: New York City Votes To Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages, Ending 170-Year Tradition
desc:
New York City Votes To Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages, Ending 170-Year Tradition

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

The New York City Council voted on Thursday to pass Romanch's Law, phasing out horse-drawn carriages in Central Park by June 1, 2028.

Forty Council members voted yes. Twenty-nine had signed onto the bill sponsored by Council Member Christopher Marte. Speaker Julie Menin is the first sitting speaker to support such a ban.

"Today, the City Council made history. Our landmark vote to pass Romanch's Law is a demonstration of this Council's commitment to animal welfare, public safety, and worker protection," Menin said in a statement.

The law bars new licenses on or after June 1, 2028. Existing ones expire permanently on May 31, 2028. The law requires the mayor's administration to create a workforce transition program by April 1, 2027, which includes job referrals, career counseling, hiring fairs, and educational opportunities.

It also considers compensation for owners based on business value, licenses, and equipment. Horses must be certified by June 1, 2027, not to be sold for slaughter or other inhumane purposes, and owners may keep them.

A joint working group will include one representative each from the speaker's office, the administration, and labor.

The vote followed the June death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, a tourist from India.

On June 17, Mahajan fell from a carriage after the horse spooked and bolted during a ride with his family. Mahajan hit his head and died. After his death, Menin announced her support for the ban in a video on X.

"The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable," Menin said Oct. 14 when announcing the Oct. 22 full council vote on the measure.

Mahajan's death was the first in more than 160 years of horse-drawn carriages operating under the Transport Workers Union, which represents the carriage drivers, in the park.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani confirmed he and the speaker had agreed to the June 1, 2028, end date.

"I think that we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani said at an unrelated press conference on Oct. 14.

The Transport Workers Union denounced the text of the bill as noncommittal, with "no meaningful economic relief for workers."

The bill does not require the city to compensate the 68 owners for their city-issued licenses or medallions.

In a statement, the union denounced Menin for what it described as using "the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis."

President Donald Trump, who is from New York City, criticized the ban on Truth Social, writing: "So sad to see the beloved Central Park Horse-drawn Carriage Industry ending after over a Century, based largely on one tragic accident. When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don't stop cars from entering the Park. So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that's gone. It will be missed!"

In a separate post, he added, "The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!"

Animal rights group New Yorkers for Clean, Livable, and Safe Streets (NYCLASS) reacted on X to the ban.

"For decades, NYCLASS fought to end cruel and dangerous horse carriages," it wrote. "It took the extraordinary courage, compassion, and unwavering leadership of Speaker Menin."

Horse-drawn carriages have operated in Central Park since 1858. They began as transportation and became a tourist attraction.

Council Member Tony Avella introduced the first ban legislation in 2007. Later efforts, including under Mayor Bill de Blasio in 2014, failed. Ryder's Law after a 2022 horse collapse also did not pass. Council Member Robert Holden reintroduced a version in November 2025 focused on workforce programs, which also stalled.

Carriage license owner Ahmet Bilici, who trained as a veterinarian in Turkey before coming to the United States in 2001, became a carriage driver to support himself as he was learning English.

The job stuck, and he's been a driver for 23 years. He said that if the City Council wanted to work with carriage drivers, drivers would be amenable, but he said the City Council just wants a ban.

"When you take this carriage from me, I am going to lose my quarter century! No way!" he previously told The Epoch Times. "I trusted the city because the city licensed the medallion, and now you are shutting down? No way!"

Bilici said the ban will hurt 300 families including support staff such as stable workers, blacksmiths producing horseshoes, and craftsmen making saddles.

"This is my small business, my investment. It's like my house. You're burning my house!" he said. "There's no way we can accept this."

Another driver, Danielle Slot, also said she was extremely disappointed. She said she thinks there is no solid justification for the ban.

"Our City Council is supposed to look out for people and represent people, and they're supposed to see through these things," Slot previously told The Epoch Times, referring to the long-term campaign of NYCLASS head Steven Nislick to ban carriage horses, which dates to 2008.

"I've just completely lost faith in the government here, which is very sad," she said. "It feels like they're capitalizing on sensationalism.

"It's a really nice thought that there would be some magical sanctuary [for the horses]. But it's just not realistic."

City rules currently limit horses to nine-hour workdays, five weeks of annual vacation, and prohibit work when temperatures are below 18 degrees or above 90 degrees.

desc:

Ukraine says its military forces continue to experience disruptions to critical battlefield communications, a day after President Trump declared that these restrictions had been removed.

"President Trump called Elon Musk on Wednesday and asked him to lift restrictions on a military-grade version of Starlink in Ukraine that the SpaceX chief had throttled, U.S. officials said," The Wall Street Journal had initially reported Thursday.

"The system was working more normally Thursday, shortly after their conversation, U.S. and Ukrainian officials said," the WSJ reported further. "Some Ukrainian officials said the system wasn't restored to full functionality but was working at higher speeds than under the cap."

But there are conflicting reports, with on Friday one prominent European source reporting the following:

Officials monitoring the systems said they continued to record instances of terminals losing connectivity when travelling at speeds of 161 kilometers per hour.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky known by his call sign Flash, confirmed that the restrictions remained in place.

"We are currently seeing no indication that the Starlink restrictions have been lifted," he wrote on Facebook on Friday.

It seems that President Trump threw Elon Musk under the bus to some extent, amid European outrage over the throttling of Starshield systems.

"I don’t comment one way or the other," Trump said on Thursday. "The bottom line: He put it back."

But again, some Ukrainian officials and reports in Western media are questioning whether service has indeed been 'put back' or fully restored. Trump and Zelensky on Friday...

  • US President Trump says if there is still a problem with Starlink in Ukraine, then he will sort it

A Friday CNBC report lays out the following while highlighting additional complaints that things have not been fully brought back online:

A group of Silicon Valley U.S. House Democrats on Friday demanded the White House investigate recent interruptions of Elon Musk’s Starlink internet service in Ukraine in a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

The letter, shared exclusively with CNBC and led by California Democratic Reps. Sam Liccardo, Ro Khanna and Jimmy Panetta, comes after Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink, was restricted in Ukraine for a period of time, limiting the besieged country’s military capabilities.

Ukrainian officials told CNN on Friday that restrictions remained in place, despite President Donald Trump’s claim Thursday that Musk had restored access. The officials said the restrictions were disrupting high-speed military drones, hampering Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attacks and conduct operations along the front line.

The letter to Wiles demands an "immediate, government-wide investigation into the decision to restrict SpaceX’s Starshield satellite-based intelligence and military support services in Ukraine."

As for whether it has been restored or not, it is curious that Zelensky himself a full week ago indicated that it had. Conflicting reports still persist at this stage.

President Donald Trump on Oct. 22 urged Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) to resign from her congressional role over allegations that she used a fake name to enter Congress.

This followed a motion filed by U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro on Oct. 21 that referred to Omar as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar." The filing was related to a federal search warrant for the congresswoman's home.

"It was just revealed that Ilhan Omar's name is not Ilhan Omar, the one she used to get elected and sworn into Congress, but rather, it's an entirely different name, Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, and that her last name is, incredibly, also the exact name of her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, the person they said she married and had children with," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

Omar addressed allegations she married her brother during a recent interview with MS NOW's Chris Hayes, calling the claims insane. When asked whether any of the allegations had a "kernel of truth," she answered: "Not to my knowledge."

"Somebody put in there that, you know, he had to have been my brother or something to that effect," she said in the interview, adding that it started on a Somali blog, without elaborating.

Omar has been married to Tim Mynett since 2020.

Trump said Omar should resign from Congress immediately, adding that she would "not be legally allowed" to remain a member of Congress from this point forward because she used "a fake name to be sworn in."

"When asked whether or not she married her brother, she said, 'Not to my knowledge.' In other words, she somehow didn't know?" Trump said.

Omar's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

Omar, a native of Somalia, moved to the United States with her family in the 1990s amid a civil war. She became a state representative in Minnesota in 2017, and a U.S. representative in 2019.

Federal agents searched the congresswoman's home in Washington on Oct. 12 as part of a criminal probe into allegations of possible immigration fraud. Federal officials have provided few details about what led to the investigation.

Omar, who is seeking a fifth term in the House of Representatives in the midterm elections, has strongly denied immigration fraud allegations.

House Democratic leaders have said that the search was politically motivated and criticized the Trump administration, noting the timing shortly before the Nov. 3 midterms.

"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said in a statement.

Border czar Tom Homan told Fox News on Oct. 17 that investigators have a strong case in their ongoing probe of Omar.

He indicated that Omar could be stripped of her U.S. citizenship and deported if the immigration fraud allegations against her are proven to be true.

"Of course, if you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We've done it before. It's a long, tedious process, but it's been done before," he said.

title: Tech Layoffs Surge As Corporate America's AI Blitz Raises Fears The Worst Is Yet To Come
desc:
Tech Layoffs Surge As Corporate America's AI Blitz Raises Fears The Worst Is Yet To Come

Bloomberg story counts featuring terms such as "job cuts," "layoffs," and "firings" jumped Thursday to their highest level since early May.

The surge in AI-related layoff announcements shows corporate America is ramping up efforts to reduce its workforce and replace humans with chatbots and other AI-related technologies to drive efficiency.

The latest headlines span American Express on Friday morning, Barclays on Thursday, and eBay and Netflix in recent days and weeks.

The AI layoffs are here: *AMERICAN EXPRESS TO CUT 5% OF JOBS, ABOUT 3,500 EMPLOYEES *BARCLAYS TO CUT 5,000 JOBS AS AI STARTS CREATING EFFICIENCY *EBAY CONFIRMS JOB CUTS OF ABOUT 9% *NETFLIX TO LAY OFF 6% OF GLOBAL STAFF, OR ABOUT 1,000 JOBS: WSJ

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 23, 2026

Separately, Yahoo Tech's Katie Teague and Valentina Palladino cite data from job tracker TrueUp showing that tech companies have cut more than 190,000 jobs this year.

The cuts in the technology space build on the 245,000 layoffs across the sector last year.

Some of the most notable cuts this year have come from Oracle, which eliminated 21,000 jobs over the past year, roughly 13% of its workforce. Oracle linked workforce reductions to its deployment of AI.

"The adoption and deployment of AI technologies across our operations have resulted, and may continue to result, in reductions to our workforce," Oracle said.

Microsoft's latest round affected 4,800 jobs, primarily in its Xbox gaming division. That followed 14,000 tech job losses in June across companies including Lucid, Bungie, and Robinhood. Samsung, Zillow, and even TikTok have pushed forward with job cuts.

The list of tech job losses below highlights increasing pressure on companies to reduce their total workforce and adopt AI and restructure operations, a trend that could accelerate into the new year:

October 2026

eBay

eBay will reportedly cut 9% of its workforce in an effort to streamline operations. The latest job cuts come after a previous round of layoffs back in February, which affected about 800 positions. "As we work to capture the significant opportunity ahead, this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," an eBay spokesperson said in a statement.

Electronic Arts (EA)

Video game publisher EA will eliminate 400 jobs, or about 3% of its workforce. This includes shutting down BioWare, the development studio behind the Mass Effect games. The next Mass Effect title will be canceled as a result of the layoffs. These job cuts come after EA told investors earlier this year that it would reduce research and development costs as part of a plan to save upward of $700 million.

Netflix

According to a report in The Wall Street Journal, Netflix will lay off about 1,000 people, accounting for about 6% of its global workforce. The report says the bulk of the layoffs will affect Netflix's "product, tech, legal and human-resources teams." This latest round of layoffs is the biggest for the company since 2022, and it comes as Netflix struggles to increase customer engagement and overall growth.

Airtable

A "large part" of the Airtable team was laid off on October 12. Federico Simionato, Airtable owner Bending Spoons' product leader, said on X that the layoffs were not due to the workers' abilities but rather to the company's "deep belief that small teams ship more and better." The exact number of employees affected by the layoffs wasn't disclosed.

Amazon

Amazon has reportedly laid off "fewer than 1,000 white-collar workers" in its stores division. That's the part of the company that oversees the tech giant's e-commerce website. Employees in the U.S., India, and the United Kingdom were reportedly affected.

Workday

Workday will lay off around 140 employees in the Bay Area as part of an effort to trim its tech team. The cuts come as part of a broader plan to cut the company's global workforce by 2.5%.

September 2026

Xbox

Xbox announced it had eliminated 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and additional areas of the Xbox Game Studios division. These layoffs are part of a "reset" it announced this summer; the company had already laid off 1,600 people in July and said at the time that an additional 1,600 terminations were still to come.

Apple

According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has laid off an undisclosed number of employees from Fitness+, the company's exercise subscription service. According to the report, the layoffs affected those who worked on the audio side of the division, which includes features like Time to Walk and Time to Run guided audio workouts. Reportedly, offerings like these will be reduced but not eliminated completely from the service.

Oracle

Oracle employees were impacted by yet another round of layoffs in September. The total number of employees laid off this time around is not currently known. The tech giant reportedly sent employees early-morning emails on Monday, September 14, letting those affected know it would be their last working day. It's also reported that, with these layoffs, Oracle is looking to offset the amount of money it is pouring into AI chips and data centers. Earlier this year, Oracle laid off 21,000 people.

Uber

Uber announced it will cut 3,300 jobs, or about 10% of its workforce, in a big restructuring effort. "We are removing layers, simplifying team structures, refining our global location strategy, and focusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in a statement. While the cuts apply to both regular employees and managers, the company stated it will reduce the "number of employees who sit 7+ layers from the CEO" by 20%, and it will cut the number of "micro-teams" by almost 50%. The CEO's memo did not mention AI as a catalyst for the layoffs, but it did explain that this restructuring will allow Uber to bring its services to more people, invest in more drivers and merchants, and "build the autonomous future."

August 2026

Apple

According to an AppleInsider report, Apple laid off at least 60 people in its Vision Group, which is the team responsible for the Vision Pro VR headset. A Bloomberg report notes that Apple is also eliminating roles in its Intelligent Systems Experience group, which is partially responsible for some of the AI systems on Apple devices. Overall, it's estimated that the layoffs affect more than 200 people.

When it comes to the Vision Group and Vision Pro, it's been reported that incoming CEO John Ternus would be putting that product category "on ice," so this seems like the start of that process. The Vision Pro headset came out in 2024 with an eye-watering $3,699 starting price, and it remains to be seen if Apple will be pulling out of the AR/VR category entirely in the future. The Intelligent Systems changes are reportedly tied to necessary changes in the technical architecture of Apple's newly AI-infused Siri.

TikTok

The New York Times reported that TikTok will lay off 250 people and close its Nashville, Tennessee, office in October. This location was home to some of TikTok's content moderation team, although the company has not specified the reason for the layoffs or which teams they primarily affect. "We have decided to close our Nashville office to streamline our operations and better align our teams for long-term growth," a press officer for what is known as the TikTok U.S.D.S. Joint Venture said in a statement to the Times.

Zillow

Zillow will lay off just over 500 people as it enacts organizational changes across the company. "These are difficult decisions that reflect both the strides we're making in our strategy and the reality of what is required of us to grow at scale," CEO Jeremy Wacksman wrote in a press release. Wacksman didn't go into detail about what organizational changes were made or which departments are bearing the brunt of the layoffs. "These changes are about ensuring we have a disciplined cost structure and getting more efficient, with the right people in the right positions," he wrote.

Etsy

Etsy laid off about 220 people, or 12% of its workforce, as it attempts to simplify its organizational structure. The cuts primarily affected the product and engineering teams, and Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said that the layoffs were necessary to build "the organization we believe Etsy needs for the future." An Etsy spokesperson told CNBC that the cuts were not driven by artificial intelligence adoption.

July 2026

Microsoft

Microsoft has begun another round of layoffs that affects 4,800 jobs, or around 2.1% of its workforce. The Xbox division is getting hit the hardest, with 3,200 roles getting cut through fiscal year 2027, Xbox chief Asha Sharma said in a post on X. A total of 1,600 people were let go on July 6. Shortly after those layoffs were revealed, it was announced that Sharma was appointed to a U.S. Federal Reserve task force to help advise it on "productivity and jobs." Other appointees include Marc Andreessen of Andreessen Horowitz and Charles I. Jones, professor of economics at Stanford University.

Intel

Intel is reportedly downsizing its data center group, despite strong performance. The company hasn't disclosed how many roles would be affected.

Visa

Visa will cut about 2,600 jobs, which amounts to about 7% of its workforce. The layoffs will primarily affect the technology and product teams, and the impetus, in part, is to make the company more efficient. "To capture the opportunities ahead and best position Visa to lead this transformation, we must continue evolving how we work," Chief Executive Officer Ryan McInerney wrote in a memo. "AI is also helping to accelerate this evolution and shape the way work gets done at Visa." But according to Bloomberg's report, AI was not the only factor to influence Visa's decision to carry out these layoffs. The company reportedly intends to reinvest in things like consumer payments and value-added services such as stablecoins.

Monday.com

Software company Monday.com will lay off 20% of its workforce, which comes out to about 630 people. This comes as the company makes a pivot to AI and is attempting to make its AI platform a core offering of its business. Earlier this year, it designed its main product around the idea that business customers increasingly want their employees to work with AI agents.

Patreon

Patreon laid off 20% of its workforce, or 93 people, as part of what it described as "changing our organizational structure and how we work." But Patreon was explicit in its email to creators and staff that "we are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans." However, the email also said, "AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, though, including how we work."

Uber

Uber has reportedly laid off 10% of its customer service division, according to a Bloomberg report, as it looks to "embrace artificial intelligence" and simplify its ranks. The company also stated in May that it would slow hiring as it makes greater internal use of AI.

Samsung

Samsung is eliminating 179 jobs as it moves its New Jersey headquarters to Texas later this year. The move is expected to impact around 1,000 workers. We're now getting a fuller picture of what that looks like: according to Reuters, 739 roles at Samsung's New Jersey location have been affected in some way. Some employees have been offered relocation packages as the company shifts its headquarters to Texas, while others have been let go. In addition, it's reported that 100 employees at its Texas location, primarily in the mobile division, have also been let go.

Amazon

Amazon will lay off some people in its artificial general intelligence group, although the company has not disclosed how many roles will be affected. "This is a fast-moving space, and we're sharpening our focus on the initiatives that matter most for customers, so we can move faster on what counts," an Amazon spokesperson told CNBC.

June 2026

Bungie

Sony Interactive Entertainment released a statement saying it's cutting "a significant number of employees" from its Bungie workforce. That includes most of the Destiny team and some Marathon team members, as well as SIE teams that support Bungie's operations. The email didn't say how many employees were affected.

Lucid

Electric vehicle maker Lucid announced it's cutting around 18% of its workforce and also noted that COO Marc Winterhoff is leaving the company, Reuters reported. The layoffs are in an effort to "boost profitability amid growing competition." The cuts affect full-time employees, contractors, and hourly manufacturing workers.

Rackspace

Cloud computing services company Rackspace laid off 750 workers, or around 15% of its workforce. The cuts are driven by a shift in focus toward AI.

Rivian

EV company Rivian let go of hundreds of employees, which amounts to around 2% of the company's workforce, The Wall Street Journal reported. Those affected were part of Rivian's service and customer organization, which handled marketing and sales.

Robinhood

Trading platform company Robinhood is planning to lay off 10% of its staff to restructure, the Robinhood Comms account said on X. That amounts to around 290 jobs. It's unclear if the layoffs are AI-related, but CEO Vlad Tenev noted the company will be "utilizing frontier technologies to push our execution even further."

Salesforce

Salesforce laid off at least 86 employees in California, though Business Insider sources say job cuts also occurred in Washington and outside the U.S.. The cuts reportedly affect employees involved with Salesforce's Agentforce AI product, MuleSoft IT integration tool, and Marketing Cloud software.

May 2026

Groupon

Groupon is planning to lay off roughly 25% of its workforce, which will result in 400 job cuts. Those positions are expected to be eliminated by the end of the third quarter. This is in an effort to restructure the company and rebuild it as an AI-native company.

Wix

In another set of AI-related layoffs, website builder Wix said it was cutting around 20% of staff. Wix co-founder and CEO Avishai Abrahami announced the cuts on X, pointing to the changes AI is bringing to the industry and stating, "we need to become a faster, leaner, and flatter organization." He also put part of the blame on the Israeli shekel-to-U.S. dollar exchange rate, which affects the company because it's based in Israel. The cuts are expected to impact around 1,000 roles, based on Wix's headcount.

Webflow

Webflow, a website builder and hosting company, conducted a round of layoffs that an employee called "a bloodbath" in a statement to the San Francisco Chronicle. It's unclear how many employees were impacted, but one anonymous developer from the company told the Chronicle they believed it was larger than Webflow's last major round of layoffs, which affected 8% of its workforce in 2024. As with other recent layoffs, it looks like a shift to AI is to blame here. "AI is rewriting the rules for how marketing teams create, test, and optimize digital experiences," CEO Linda Tong said in a statement. "And the companies that move decisively through moments like this are the ones that come out ahead."

ClickUp

ClickUp CEO Zeb Evans announced that the company cut 22% of its workforce as it turns toward AI to improve productivity. He claimed it "wasn't about cutting costs," but about funneling savings from the cuts "directly back into the people who stay." The company has introduced million-dollar salary bands reserved for employees who "create outsized impact using AI."

Intuit

Intuit is planning to lay off 3,000 employees, or about 17% of its workforce, Reuters reports. CEO Sasan Goodarzi sent a memo to employees noting the layoffs would help the company's efforts to infuse AI across its services.

Meta

Meta has officially begun cutting 10% of its workforce, totaling around 8,000 employees. In addition, it plans to close 6,000 open roles. The reason is to allow more room for AI spending.

NPR

Like Microsoft, NPR is offering voluntary buyouts to 300 employees in the newsroom, but only 30 will be accepted. However, if the news organization doesn't reach its target number of buyouts, it will conduct targeted layoffs. The cuts are due to the loss of federal funding.

Amazon

The online retail giant cut more jobs this month, this time from the Selling Partner Services organization. These new layoffs come after Amazon cut roughly 30,000 jobs in rounds in October and January. A spokesperson told Business Insider that the most recent layoffs have affected a "small number" of employees. The Selling Partner Services team works with third-party merchants on Amazon, providing onboarding, logistics, and account management support.

Cisco

Cisco is cutting just under 4,000 jobs in Q4, CEO Chuck Robbins said in a blog post. Impacted employees will receive prorated payments of their 2026 bonuses and will also receive "support in finding new opportunities" via Cisco's placement services. In June, it was confirmed that the layoffs include 471 workers in the Bay Area.

"While we are reducing roles in some areas, we are making clear, strategic investments, particularly in silicon, optics, security, and in our employees' use of AI across the company," Robbins said.

LinkedIn

LinkedIn is planning to lay off 5% of its staff, which is around 875 employees, Reuters reports. An anonymous person told Reuters the reason is to reorganize teams and focus employees on areas where its business is growing. However, one of the sources said the reason was "not for artificial intelligence to replace jobs at LinkedIn."

General Motors

GM is letting go of around 500 to 600 employees in the information technology sector, Bloomberg reports. The reason is to "trim costs and clear the way to bring in staff with skills in other technology areas."

Cloudflare

Due to restructuring driven by AI, Cloudflare is laying off more than 1,100 employees. "Today's actions are not a cost-cutting exercise or an assessment of individuals' performance; They are about Cloudflare defining how a world-class, high-growth company operates and creates value in the agentic AI era," Prince and President Michelle Zatlyn said in an email to employees.

PayPal

PayPal is planning to cut around 20% of its staff, or nearly 4,800 employees, over the next few years, according to The Wall Street Journal. "First, we will remove duplication and layers from our organizational structure. Second, we will accelerate our AI adoption and automation across our operations," CEO Enrique Lores said to investors.

Coinbase

Cryptocurrency platform Coinbase is laying off 700 employees, which amounts to around 14% of its staff. CEO Brian Armstrong cites current market conditions and AI-driven changes in how the company works as reasons for the layoffs.

April 2026

Microsoft

Microsoft is offering a first-ever buyout to up to 7% of its employees, CNBC reports. It's a one-time retirement program that's available for workers at the senior director level and below whose combined age and years of employment total 70 or more.

Nike

Nike announced it's laying off 1,400 people this week. "Collectively, these changes will result in a reduction of approximately 1,400 roles in global operations, with the majority in technology," COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy said. "These reductions are very hard for the teammates directly affected and for the teams around them, too."

Amazon

Amazon is planning to temporarily close a warehouse in Homestead, Florida, which will eliminate more than 600 jobs, Newsweek reports. The job cuts will start in July and continue through September, but the company is giving employees the option to relocate to other facilities. The warehouse has only been open for just under two years, but Amazon is already looking to update the site.

Redwood Materials

Battery recycling company Redwood Materials laid off 10% of its employees, totaling 135 people, TechCrunch reports. Those who were let go received an email from the chief HR officer telling them the layoffs were made "to sharpen our focus, our work and the size of our teams to support the direction Redwood is going in the future."

Snap

Snap is laying off 1,000 workers, which is 16% of its staff, Variety reports. The Snapchat parent company made the announcement just weeks after Irenic Capital Management asked the company to make changes to improve performance and revenue.

Snap is using AI to streamline operations and assist the now-smaller workforce. "We have already witnessed small squads leveraging AI tools to drive meaningful progress across several important initiatives," Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said.

Disney

Just two months after taking over as CEO of Disney, Josh D'Amaro announced the company is laying off 1,000 of its employees, AP News reports. In addition, Marvel let 8% of its staff go after the call was made.

"Over the past several months, we have looked at ways in which we can streamline our operations in various parts of the company to ensure we deliver the world-class creativity and innovation our fans value and expect from Disney," D'Amaro said in a memo to employees. "Given the fast-moving pace of our industries, this requires us to constantly assess how to foster a more agile and technologically-enabled workforce to meet tomorrow's needs."

GoPro

The wearable camera maker will eliminate 145 positions this year due to a restructuring plan to cut costs, The Wall Street Journal reported. The cuts are expected to last until the end of the year.

Vimeo

Vimeo is going through its third round of layoffs since it was acquired by Bending Spoons. This time, the company let go of more than 120 people, which is about 25% of its city staff.

Meta

It's been reported that 200 Meta employees in the Bay Area will lose their jobs at the end of May. That includes 124 employees in Burlingame and 74 in Sunnyvale. The company last laid off workers just a few weeks ago.

March 2026

Oracle

Oracle has begun implementing a big cull of its employee base. On the final day of March, more than a dozen Oracle employees announced on LinkedIn they had been let go from their jobs, Business Insider reports. It's unclear at this time how many workers were affected, but it was projected to be thousands at the start of this month.

Those laid off received the same email: "After careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change."

The job cuts are reportedly to help Oracle stem a cash drain related to its expenditures on AI infrastructure. In June, Oracle revealed that it had laid off 21,000 people as part of the cuts.

Eidos-Montréal

Deus Ex studio Eidos-Montréal announced on March 30 that it's laying off 124 people. In response, studio head David Anfossi has decided to leave the company.

The cuts are a result of "changing project needs and impacts across production and support teams," the gaming company said in a LinkedIn post. It also noted that the decision to lay off these employees is not related to their talent or performance.

T-Mobile

After already having layoffs in January, T-Mobile has cut even more of its workers, GeekWire reports. It's unclear how many people were laid off at this time, but it could be in the hundreds.

"To move even faster in a dynamic market while continuing to deliver best-in-class digital experiences for our customers, we're further aligning our IT organization to support future growth and innovation… This includes the difficult decision of eliminating some roles while continuing to invest and hire in areas," T-Mobile told GeekWire in a statement.

Meta

Meta began laying off hundreds of employees on March 25, totaling around 700 people, per The New York Times. Those impacted were part of the Reality Labs team, as well as social media and recruiting teams. Though still significant, this is a much smaller number compared to a Reuters report that suggested 20% of staff would be affected by layoffs due to the increased spending on AI.

This change comes as the company is shifting away from its metaverse creation, which includes Horizon Worlds for its Quest VR headset that's operated by the Reality Labs team.

Epic Games

The gaming giant on March 24 announced it was laying off more than 1,000 workers in an effort to right-size the staff of its popular free-to-play online shooter, Fortnite. CEO Tim Sweeney sent a note to his staff, citing the "downturn in Fortnite engagement," which means "we're spending significantly more than we're making, and we have to make major cuts to keep the company funded." He made it a point to note the layoffs are not related to AI.

Ubisoft

Ubisoft laid off 105 employees from the Red Storm Entertainment team in an effort to cut costs, IGN reports. Game development has ended at the studio, so the downsizing will remain permanent. The company employed 180 people in 2022 but has seen multiple layoffs over the years.

Atlassian

Roughly 1,600 employees were laid off at Atlassian on March 16, which is around 10% of total workers. Ahead of the layoffs, Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes shared a message with the entire team, letting them know the reason was to "self-fund further investment in AI and enterprise sales, while strengthening our financial profile. We're also changing the way we work and reorganising around our System of Work to move faster." Impacted employees received an email shortly after this message went out.

Together, this all shows an acceleration by corporate America to streamline operations and improve productivity in the era of AI.

title: Main St.-Wall St. Divide Reaches Record High As UMich Inflation Angst Re-Accelerates
desc:
Main St.-Wall St. Divide Reaches Record High As UMich Inflation Angst Re-Accelerates

Preliminary October UMich Sentiment held steady this month, registering a tiny 0.1pt decline below September (Current Condiutions dipped but Expectations ticked up)...

Increases in sentiment among Republicans and Democrats were balanced by declines among independents.

While year-ahead business conditions improved about 14%, they stand 16% less than last October’s read.

This month’s decline in the Current Conditions subindex was driven entirely by buying conditions for durables, which plunged 18% on the basis of higher interest rates and rising concerns about the affordability of such purchases.

Inflation expectations over both time horizons increased for the second straight month to their highest readings since May.

  • Long-run inflation expectations also stepped up from 3.4% in September to 3.5%, notably higher than their 2024 range of 2.8% to 3.2%.

  • Year-ahead inflation expectations ticked up from 4.6% last month to 4.7% this month.

Frustration over high prices eroding consumers’ living standards continues to mount.

For the fourth straight month, an increasing share of consumers spontaneously mentioned that high prices are dragging down their personal finances, at 56% this month, compared with 45% in January of this year. As seen in the chart below, these increases are seen across the political spectrum, with Republicans exhibiting the largest proportional rise. In contrast, the wealthiest consumers report little change in the burden of high prices since January. Gasoline prices remain highly salient this month, mentioned unprompted by over 40% of respondents.

Purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy.

Sentiment is now 10% below a year ago and 15% less than February, just prior to the Iran conflict.

Finally, some crazy context, Wall Street (S&P 500 Total Return Index) has surged to record levels, while the Main Street (UMich Consumer Sentiment) has plunged near its all-time low...

This gap reflects a market powered by corporate profits, tech concentration, and investor optimism even as households report deep frustration over high prices, borrowing costs, and weakened current economic conditions (which hit a record low of 44.7). Such extremes have historically been rare and highlight how equity markets and everyday consumer experiences have decoupled.

title: US Manufacturing Sector Survey Hits 53-Month High, But "Cost Pressures Remain Key Concern"
desc:
US Manufacturing Sector Survey Hits 53-Month High, But "Cost Pressures Remain Key Concern"

After surging in September (and prompting some exciting moves in Treasuries - and STIRs), preliminary October PMIs from S&P Global were expected to drop modestly (for both Manufacturing and Services).

Instead it was more mixed with Manufacturing better than expected (56.0 vs 55.9 prior vs 55.5 exp) but Services down a little (57.9 vs 58.8 prior vs 58.0 exp).

That is a 53-month high for the Manufacturing sector...

The US remains the strongest economy in the world based on these surveys...

“October’s flash PMI data indicate that the US economy continues to boom at the start of the fourth quarter," according to Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The output readings from the survey are consistent with GDP growing at a 5% annualized rate after a 4% expansion was signalled for the third quarter.

Especially healthy corporate earnings and profits are also indicated, and hiring has surged as companies seek to boost capacity to fulfil stronger customer demand.

“If the reopening of the economy after COVID is excluded, recent months have seen the best growth spell for US businesses since early 2015."

However, Williamson notes that "cost pressures remain a key concern, notably as the renewed surge in oil prices reverberates through to impact a wide variety of goods and services."

Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers.

The result is the sharpest increase in selling prices for over four years to a pace that indicates consumer price inflation is likely to rise further above the Fed’s target in the coming months.

Not a good signal for The Fed next week.

title: New Trump Peace Plan Outline For Ukraine Emerges
desc:
New Trump Peace Plan Outline For Ukraine Emerges

Ukrainian media is widely reporting that a key aspect of the US peace proposal heading into agreed-to trilateral talks, likely to come sometime in November, is that Ukraine would permanently abandon its bid to join the NATO alliance and in exchange it would be offered European Union membership.

Additionally, a demilitarized zone in the Donbass is envisioned, along with a resumption of Russian gas supplies to Europe and via Nord Stream. The alleged new details in the plan, which haven't been officially confirmed by the Trump administration, were first outlined in The Economist.

Further, other economic incentives are said to include commercial agreements between Moscow and American companies, sanctions relief, and of course fully restored political ties with Washington.

The full list of alleged details in the plan is being reported by Ukrainian media citing Ukrainian officials in The Economist. The new Trump peace plan includes:

  • Demilitarized zone in Donbas
  • Ukraine abandons NATO
  • Investment package & EU membership for Ukraine
  • Russian business deals with US companies, lifting sanctions & normalization of political relations
  • Resumptions of Russian gas supplies to Europe & Nord Stream

Details have yet to be handed from Washington to the Ukrainian side, but reportedly only a draft outline has been circulating, coming at a time Zelensky is under immense pressure and criticism from the Trump White House.

According to Kyiv Post, in reference to The Economist, "One Ukrainian official told the magazine that Kyiv fears US representatives could pursue lucrative deals with Moscow before the war ends, allowing Russia to gain economic and diplomatic benefits while fighting continues."

President Zelensky has meanwhile vented his frustration in a fresh interview, saying:

title: SK Hynix Scraps Solidigm IPO, Single-Handedly Drags Kospi Out Of A 4% Hole And Easing AI Rout
desc:
SK Hynix Scraps Solidigm IPO, Single-Handedly Drags Kospi Out Of A 4% Hole And Easing AI Rout

Last night we were fairly confident how the Korean session would go.

Three hours until Korea is halted seconds after the open

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 22, 2026

Well, we were half right. The Kospi did crater at the open, sliding as much as 4.1% and more than halfway to triggering a market halt as Asia digested the overnight carnage in US tech (SOX -6.7%, META -7.0%). And then, over the course of the session, it climbed all the way back and closed green, up 0.30% at 5,550.

What changed? Well, according to Bloomberg, the biggest AI news out of Asia overnight was that SK Hynix scrapped plans for a potential $10 billion US listing of its Solidigm unit after facing strong opposition from regulators and shareholders. SK Hynix shares, which had dropped as much as 4.3% early, immediately reversed and rallied as much as 4.5% on the news, defying a broad market slide triggered by the rout in US tech.

SK Hynix Pulls Solidigm’s $10 Billion IPO on Regulatory Pushback: BBG

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 23, 2026

Seoul Says No To The "Duplicate Listing"

The retreat followed domestic regulatory scrutiny over concerns that Solidigm's IPO could dilute share value for SK Hynix's minority investors and complicate SK Group's ownership structure. In a Friday regulatory filing, the company also halted talks on a pre-IPO investment, citing - what else - "recent capital market conditions."

The deal was meant to be a monster. Solidigm, one of the world's largest makers of the flash memory used for storage in AI data centers (it was carved out of Intel's NAND and SSD business, which SK Hynix bought in 2021), had already picked banks including Goldman and Morgan Stanley and was looking to raise about $10 billion as soon as next year, at a valuation of as much as $100 billion. When the spin first hit the tape last month, Goldman's TMT specialist desk was passing along talk of a valuation of "up to $150bn", which tells you how hot things were running just four weeks ago.

Investors in the parent never liked it. When the IPO reports first hit on Sept 28, Hynix fell 5.0%, and Goldman's Korea desk noted that "local reports attributed today's weakness in Hynix to headlines that said its US subsidiary Solidigm is considering a US IPO as soon as next year," with foreigners dumping $1.27 billion of the stock that day. The math is simple enough: why own the parent at a big discount when the crown jewel is about to list separately in New York, with the family controlling both?

The regulators, it turned out, agreed. In its Oct 19 open, Goldman's Seoul desk flagged that the FSC governor said "both the FSC and FSS judge that Solidigm falls under the restriction on duplicate listing," the same morning President Lee said the government "should press ahead with efforts to improve corporate governance." Once Seoul had openly made Solidigm a test case for the "Korea discount" crusade, the IPO was probably dead on arrival.

Governance activists were thrilled. Namuh Rhee, chair of the Korean Corporate Governance Forum, called it "great news" and "a sign that the company is aware of conflict of interest between Chairman Chey and minority shareholders." Terton Capital's Ryan Albert called it "a major positive for Korean corporate governance."

Not a sentence you often read about a chaebol.

One Stock, One Green Close

So did the Solidigm reversal save the Kospi? The Goldman Korea desk's closing wrap (available to pro subs) makes it pretty clear who did the heavy lifting:

KOSPI grinded higher after falling as much as -4.1% in the early morning, eventually closing +30bps. The recovery was mainly led by SK HYNX(000660) +4.4%, while most other sectors still finished lower (weak breadth with 719 declining vs. 173 advancing in KOSPI) as risk off sentiment persisted amid geopolitical tensions and fragile sentiment toward Tech.

Translation: more than four stocks fell for every one that rose, and the index still closed green (a mirror image of what happened in the US the day before). Goldman's regional wrap said the same thing, noting Korea "recovered from a 4.1% intraday decline to close 0.30% higher, driven by SK Hynix, although breadth remained weak." Samsung helped a little, closing +0.5% after being down as much as 5.1%.

There is a wrinkle, though. The Solidigm filing came out before the open, and Goldman's morning call still had Kospi futures -2.6% with Korea "poised to extend its losses." Hynix then dropped 4.3% anyway before turning higher, and the desk says the chipmakers recovered "despite no fresh intraday catalyst (appeared partially driven by local insto bids)." In other words, the IPO news gave Hynix a reason to rally, while the actual buying came from Korean institutions:

Flow-wise, foreigners were net sellers in both Hynix (-$422mn) and Sammy (-$152mn), while local instos were net buyers (+$450mn in Hynix and +$102mn in Sammy). Retail investors were more on the sidelines today in the chipmakers, ending as marginal net sellers in Hynix (-$12mn) and net buyers in Sammy (+$2.5mn).

Across the whole market, foreigners were the only net sellers at -$729 million (of which -$672 million in tech), local institutions bought +$655 million, and retail - once the most feared dip-buying army on the planet - added a rounding error of +$22 million. Turnover ran 16.2% below the 20-day average. That is a very specific kind of rally: foreigners selling into domestic institutional bids on light volume.

Maybe that was just Korean pension and insurance money seeing value in Hynix. Maybe it was something a bit more... encouraged. The same morning, Goldman's regional wrap credited China's surge (CSI 300 +1.7%, ChiNext +4.0%) to "state-backed 'national team' ETF buying" with RMB84 billion of turnover across nine favored ETFs, and Indonesia's fourth straight gain to Danantara sovereign fund support. Asia, it seems, has decided it will not go down quietly with the Nasdaq. Whatever the source, the regulator's success in killing the Solidigm deal gave local buyers a convenient headline to lean on.

Supply Destruction, IPO Edition

There's a broader reason the market cheered the death of a $10 billion deal, and Goldman's EMEA head of one-delta trading Richard Privorotsky spelled it out in his flow and positioning observations this morning (available to pro subs):

Perhaps we're overthinking the concerns around AI demand and the issue is simply a repricing of the cost of capital. The assumption of effectively unlimited cheap capital to fund this buildout is being challenged. You either cut capex, delay deployment or increasingly fund through equity. None are particularly supportive of equity prices.

A $10 billion AI storage IPO sits squarely in the "fund through equity" bucket, and the market just watched one disappear. Solidigm also joins data center developers Firmus Grid and AirTrunk on the list of high-profile deals suspended or cancelled as AI bubble fears roil markets, while OpenAI is reportedly now targeting a $1.25 trillion valuation in its latest $30 billion round, down from $1.4 trillion. Back in Seoul, data center infrastructure name Elice dropped 32% in its trading debut this week, the worst opening day ever for a sizeable Korean listing. In this tape, the best IPO is the one that doesn't happen.

The AI casualty list is getting longer by the week:

As for Korea, Privorotsky admitted he was braced for worse:

Korea is actually holding up better than I would have expected given the acute liquidation across Europe and the US (Kospi flickering green having been down a lot on open)... Putting my trading hat on, I expected Korea to be down another mid-single digits this morning. The fact that we're not seeing another complete air pocket is encouraging.

He was not alone (see our tweet above). Goldman's Asia sales trader Peter Sheren also argued in "Stress Without Capitulation" that October's drawdown looks like "a concentrated positioning/technical reset rather than systemic capitulation," with GS desk flows "active but largely balanced and rotational." Korea, notably, was a net buy on the desk on Friday:

Sheren also points out the concentration problem every EM manager is wrestling with: TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix together account for more than 30% of MSCI EM. When one of the three gets a governance-friendly headline on a day like this, an index can flip on its own.

The Buyback Is Done, The DRAM Price Isn't

Context matters here, because Hynix needed the win. The stock had plunged about 60% from its June peak before today, a slide that accelerated right after the company completed its $26.5 billion ADR listing in July, the biggest US listing by a foreign company ever. Regular readers will recall we asked at the time whether SK Hynix's US debut was the AI bubble top (Jul 11); two days later the stock suffered its steepest decline on record, sending the Kospi down as much as 9%.

Then came South Korea's biggest-ever "buyback bazooka" in August, which for a while was the only thing holding the market together. As we said in September, once retail fled, only record buybacks were preventing a Kospi crash. Earlier this month, the bid vanished:

The only thing that was propping up the Kospi in the past months is ending: the frenzied, record buyback spree by Samsung and SK Hynix is now over, earlier than expected, as it was running far faster than expected: 55 trillion won in stock bought back. Kospi closed at the lows.

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 7, 2026

Goldman's Asia macro sales desk confirms in its Asia FX Weekly (available to pro subs) that SK Hynix is "finishing its 40 trillion won buyback early and preparing further returns on Oct 28." So the next shareholder-friendly catalyst is barely a week away, and cancelling a dilutive spin right before it doesn't hurt the pitch.

Meanwhile, the fundamentals that made Hynix a $679 billion company keep heading the other way from the stock. As Russell Clark notes in his latest Capital Flows and Asset Markets note, "SK Hynix has typically been pretty responsive to spot DRAM prices. Not for the last three months." His chart shows the DDR5 spot price still grinding to new highs while Hynix shares have collapsed (perhaps this simply means that real DDR5 prices are far lower than represented by yet another gamed index):

Since November 2024, DRAM spot is up more than 1,000% versus 530% for Hynix shares, and as recently as June the stock was running well ahead of memory prices. Bank of Korea Governor Shin, per Goldman's FX desk, is "brushing off KOSPI softness given robust DRAM prices." Clark himself admits that "starting from a point of 'equities are wrong' is a recipe for disaster," which is about as honest a disclaimer as you'll find this month.

A Governance Win In A Market Still Looking For A Floor

The cancellation is good news for Hynix shareholders: no duplicate listing, no dilution of the parent's economic interest, no parent-subsidiary discount. Fibonacci Asset Management's Jung In Yun said as much, and Seoul gets a clean win for its "Korea discount" campaign.

But let's not confuse one stock's governance win with a bottom. Breadth was dreadful, foreigners sold for yet another day, Kospi turnover was light, and the index closed at 5,550 - down from 6,890 on Sept 28, when it was falling on the very Solidigm headline it rallied on today. In other words, the Kospi has lost about a fifth of its value in less than a month, and Friday's "rescue" came from local institutions bidding up the one name with a fresh catalyst. Next week brings the hyperscaler earnings that Privorotsky calls "critical," plus Hynix's Oct 28 shareholder return update. Until then, we'd lean toward this being a governance pop inside an ongoing AI deleveraging rather than the start of something bigger.

Then again, after we called for a halt at the open and got a green close instead, we'll leave the Korea predictions to the national teams for now.

Much more in the full GS Korea Final, and Privorotsky's "GS flow and positioning observations" notes, all available to pro subs.

title: Trump Invokes Defense Production Act To Increase Petroleum Production
desc:
Trump Invokes Defense Production Act To Increase Petroleum Production

Authored by Timothy Frudd via The Epoch Times,

President Donald Trump invoked the Defense Production Act of 1950 in a memorandum on Oct. 22 to increase oil production in the United States as prices remain elevated amid the Iran conflict.

In Thursday's memorandum, Trump determined that ensuring the United States had a resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity was essential for national defense.

The memorandum directed Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to complete purchases, make commitments, and use financial instruments to expand domestic petroleum infrastructure, including exploration and production, storage, marine terminals, and gathering and transmission pipelines.

"Petroleum fuels the Nation's Armed Forces, industrial base, and crucial infrastructure," Trump wrote. "Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption."

The Defense Production Act, which was enacted during the Cold War, gives the president authority over the domestic industrial base in the interest of national security. Under the legislation, the president can incentivize the domestic industrial base to increase the production and supply of critical goods and materials through direct purchases, purchase commitments, loans, and loan guarantees.

Trump's memorandum said the fastest and most cost-effective ways to meet the energy demands needed for U.S. national security are the purchases, commitments, and financial support made possible under the Defense Production Act.

The president previously issued Executive Order 14156 in January 2025, declaring a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act. At the time, Trump said that America's energy production, refining, transportation, and generation capacity was inadequate and represented an "unusual and extraordinary threat" to both the economy and U.S. national security.

Trump cited the January 2025 executive order in his memorandum to Hegseth on Thursday. The memorandum said the United States would not be able to provide the energy capabilities needed in a timely manner without taking action under the Defense Production Act due to supply chain limitations, financing constraints, infrastructure and permitting bottlenecks, and lengthy lead times.

In the memorandum, Trump said expanding petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity "is necessary to avert an industrial resource or critical technology item shortfall that would severely impair national defense capability."

The president also waived standard statutory requirements under the Defense Production Act, citing the need to expand that capacity.

Last week, Vice President JD Vance announced that the Trump administration was planning to use the Defense Production Act to expand fuel production at a petroleum refinery in Tyler, Texas, owned by Delek US Holdings.

"We want millions of gallons of commercial-grade and military-spec fuel to come out of this refinery, in addition to what it's already producing," he said.

Trump previously invoked the Defense Production Act in April and issued multiple memoranda to increase domestic coal supply chains, liquefied natural gas capacity, and natural gas transmission.

The Trump administration's use of the Defense Production Act on Thursday came as oil prices have significantly increased since the start of the Iran war in February. As of Thursday, the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, was more than $113 per barrel.

In addition, the average cost for a gallon of regular gasoline in the United States was $4.27, while the average cost for a gallon of diesel was $6.30 on Thursday, according to AAA.

Trump accused Iran on Thursday of attempting to increase oil prices ahead of the November midterm elections.

"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," Trump wrote in a statement on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
