title: SpaceX Targets 80,000 Cell Sites To Challenge Telecom Giants As Wall Street Weighs In
desc:
SpaceX Targets 80,000 Cell Sites To Challenge Telecom Giants As Wall Street Weighs In

Elon Musk is accelerating plans to build a fourth major nationwide wireless carrier, with SpaceX seeking access to at least 80,000 US cell sites, according to Bloomberg News. The prospect of a new rival to AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile lifted tower stocks in premarket trading, while shares of those legacy carriers fell as traders continued to assess that new emerging competitive threat.

The report stated that SpaceX is in talks with a number of tower companies, including Crown Castle, which, along with American Tower Corp. and Vertical Bridge Holdings, is among the largest owners of cellular towers.

"You can assume that we're talking to all parties," Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said Wednesday when asked about discussions with SpaceX, Amazon and other satellite telecommunications providers.

Crown Castle shares jumped as much as 10% in late trading following the report, while AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile each fell about 5%.

The report follows news earlier this month that SpaceX acquired low-band spectrum and received Federal Communications Commission approval to launch 15,000 satellites designed to connect directly to smartphones.

This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 8, 2026

Leasing tower space would establish ground coverage, including in buildings, under bridges, in homes, and in places where satellite coverage is ineffective. The satellites would help bridge gaps in tower coverage in remote places and areas without obstructions.

"We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there's broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk told investors on an earnings call earlier this week. He said satellite launches and spectrum purchases would put Starlink Mobile on the path to become a major US carrier.

"Whether SpaceX ultimately leases anything close to that figure remains uncertain, but the reported scope suggests a far greater level of commitment than spectrum accumulation alone. AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile shares are trading down in after-hours trading, adding to an already difficult year for the group," Bernstein analyst Laurent Yoon wrote in a note.

Separately, BNP Paribas analyst Sam McHugh offered his first take:

Would this be good enough to compete in wireless?

The 80,000-tower figure is at the upper end of the telcos' tower counts (TMUS has c. 85k, alongside c. 60k small cells). If SpaceX did build out to this many sites, even with the limited spectrum it has today, the service would be somewhat comparable to that of the existing carriers, given that it would start with no customers loading the network. However, it would not be capable of matching the existing carriers when loaded with millions of subscribers. This also somewhat undermines the argument that SpaceX can have a structural cost advantage by using its satellites for coverage or pursuing a more "femto or small cell" strategy, which, in a roundabout way, is one positive to take from these headlines.

Do we think they will do it?

It depends on what "It" is… Replicating the wireless carriers' networks (towers, spectrum, distribution, etc.) from scratch looks like a mammoth exercise, with very questionable payback for the company. So why would SpaceX do this? We do think it has a long-term ambition to build a more upload-focused network to complement its satellites that can provide connectivity to edge / physical AI (cars, robots, etc.). If, along the way, it can make enough noise and scare a telco into giving it an MVNO, then that would be a big win for SpaceX.

Would they buy instead?

In addition, by talking down the industry and depressing multiples, SpaceX creates additional optionality/upside on potential acquisitions, which, in our view, is a much clearer path to value creation (with TMUS potentially being the most credible target). It also recently acquired X and Cursor, showing it is more than willing to buy to accelerate its ambitions.

MVNO pressure?

As we wrote in Further SpaceX Spectrum Thoughts, our view is that we are past the point at which one of the carriers would fold and give SpaceX an MVNO. All that would do is help facilitate a more economical buildout for SpaceX, as it would allow the company to start generating revenue today, prove the business case, and then begin targeting investment in areas with high subscriber density. Without an MVNO/roaming deal, however, SpaceX will have to substantially build out a network before having a reasonable product proposition for customers, massively depressing the IRR.

What to watch for next?

  • Given that the telcos are unlikely to budge and SpaceX has time on its hands (buildout obligations are long-dated), we continue to think this uncertainty will persist until at least the Upper-C band auction in April next year, when SpaceX will have the opportunity to put incremental capital to work to prove its commitment to a consumer-focused mobile network (as opposed to its existing spectrum holdings, which are probably better suited to an IoT-like service).

  • If SpaceX does sign a tower deal, how many sites are covered and for what duration will be critical to assessing its ambitions.

  • Another spectrum deal (SpaceX or someone else). There are pockets of spectrum still out there that SpaceX or the telcos could move on before the C-Band auction (details at the bottom of this note), and the risk here is that SpaceX acquires more, or a telco acquires more defensively.

  • SpaceX touted the possibility of hosting an investor call to outline more specifics of its wireless ambitions soon. No firm event has been confirmed yet.

  • We continue to field questions around "Title 3 data roaming" requirements in the US, a topic we addressed earlier this year. See SpaceX's Backdoor MVNO: Expert Call Takeaways. We think this is a dead end for SpaceX. Still, after the midterms, we do see a scenario where SpaceX potentially tries to bring legal action against the telcos on the basis of a "concerted refusal to deal", or perhaps attacks the satellite JV (SpaceX) as a way to exert more pressure. Indeed, the SpaceX CFO referred to the telcos as a cartel at a public investor conference in September.

title: Futures Wobble After AI Bloodbath As Brent Hits $114, France Braces For Moody's
desc:
Futures Wobble After AI Bloodbath As Brent Hits $114, France Braces For Moody's

US futures are lower, erasing a modest overnight bounce, as markets scramble after Thursday's violent AI liquidation while oil rises again: Brent hit the highest level since May after the Houthis fired another missile at Riyadh and an IRGC official declared traffic of "illicit" vessels through Hormuz "completely stopped" (contradicted by a Bloomberg headline just minutes prior), while Thursday's haven bid fades; as a result Treasuries give back part of their biggest rally in more than two years with the 10Y yield rising back to 4.99%. As of 8:00am ET, S&P futures are down 0.2% at 7,687 while Nasdaq futures are down 0.1% at 29,100; Dow futures underperform, sliding 0.6%. That follows Thursday's chaotic session, when the S&P dropped 1.2% and the Nasdaq 100 tumbled almost 3%, its worst day since June, even as two-thirds of the S&P rose and the hedge fund VIP basket suffered its worst day since 2011 (as we detailed last night). In premarket trading, Mag 7 names are mixed with Nvidia (+0.6%) and Tesla (+0.8%) higher while Meta and Microsoft (both -0.7%) lag; tower companies jump and wireless carriers slide after SpaceX was said to be targeting 80,000 or more US cell sites, while Deckers tumbles after cutting its full-year sales guidance. The day's driver is the AI trade (what else): OpenAI is now targeting a $1.25 trillion valuation for its $30 billion raise, $150 billion below last month's ask, and SK Hynix scrapped a US listing of its Solidigm unit, yet chips are modestly higher after the Kospi erased a 4.1% plunge to close up 0.3%; according to Bloomberg, "this looks less like capitulation than a repricing of who pays for the build-out." Bonds are cheaper across the curve in a bear-flattening move, as the tech rout eases and oil climbs further, complicating the inflation outlook; French bonds outperform after the OAT-Bund spread opened at a fresh post-2011 high of 176bps, even as France's flash PMIs collapsed into contraction ahead of tonight's Moody's review. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is up 0.1% and the euro slips 0.2% after the dismal French PMI, while the kiwi outperforms on ANZ calling for three RBNZ hikes. In commodities, WTI rises 1.8% to $101.22 and Brent 1.4% to $114.80; gold is flat near $4,030 and silver slides 1.1%. Bitcoin rises 0.5% to about $81,600. US economic data slate includes the October S&P Global flash PMIs (9:45am), the final October University of Michigan sentiment and inflation expectations (10am) and the Kansas City Fed services survey (11am). The Fed is in its blackout period ahead of next Wednesday's FOMC, so there are no Fed speakers.

In premarket trading, Mag 7 stocks are mixed (Alphabet (GOOGL) -0.2%, Amazon (AMZN) -0.2%, Apple (AAPL) -0.1%, Meta Platforms (META) -0.5%, Microsoft (MSFT) -0.5%, Nvidia (NVDA) +0.2%, Tesla (TSLA) +0.1%)

  • Tower companies gain and wireless carriers slide after SpaceX was said to be targeting 80,000 or more US cell sites, with talks under way with at least one infrastructure owner. Crown Castle (CCI) +9%, American Tower (AMT) +6%; AT&T (T) -4%, T-Mobile (TMUS) -4%, Verizon (VZ) -3.8%
  • Autoliv (ALV) falls 5% after the maker of airbag systems cut its adjusted operating margin forecast for the full year.
  • Bloom Energy (BE), which has more than doubled this year on demand for AI power sources, is down 3% after its quarterly report. Bloomberg Intelligence notes that “operating cash flow turned negative in 3Q as contract assets, receivables and inventory rose.”
  • Deckers Outdoor (DECK) falls 7% after the footwear company cut its net sales guidance for the full year, which also fell short of the consensus estimate.
  • MaxLinear (MXL) climbs 2% after the semiconductor device company’s third-quarter results beat expectations and it gave a revenue forecast that is seen as strong.
  • Newmont Corp. (NEM) inches 1% lower after the miner forecast higher than expected 2027 spending for its Red Chris copper-gold mine in British Columbia.
  • Norwegian Cruise (NCLH) slips 3% after JPMorgan downgraded the stock to underweight and reduced his price target to a Street-low $11 per share. Norwegian is due to report third-quarter results on Oct. 29.
  • RingCentral (RNG) rises 16% after the communications software company raised its full-year forecast for adjusted earnings. It also reported third-quarter results that beat expectations.

In other corporate news, OpenAI's valuation ambitions got a $150 billion haircut: the ChatGPT maker is now targeting $1.25 trillion in the final stages of negotiations for its roughly $30 billion funding round, led by UAE investors, down from the $1.4 trillion it was seeking last month (good thing Anthropic is reportedly aiming for $2 trillion in its IPO). SK Hynix scrapped plans for a potential $10 billion US listing of its Solidigm unit. American Express raised its full-year EPS forecast to $18.30-$18.60 from $17.30-$17.90. BASF is said to have raised its bid for rival Evonik to about €24 per share, and SLB sees growth driven by a Middle East oil field recovery. Citigroup won approval to launch a wholly-owned securities business in China after a nearly five-year wait. Nvidia invested in AI video and image generator Higgsfield. Alnylam reported positive data for its Huntington's disease drug. Calpers is pivoting from US tech giants to private equity, the FT reports. Canadian oil and gas producer Logan Energy is exploring options including a potential sale, while allergy and autoimmune biotech Lycia Therapeutics raised $317.5 million in an upsized IPO priced at the top of its range. Apple's $2,000-and-up foldable iPhone Duo went on sale today, with new orders being offered delivery at the end of January. Infosys narrowed its FY revenue growth outlook to 1%-2% from 1.5%-3%, and China's Cambricon reported 3Q revenue of 3.53 billion yuan, well below the 6.26 billion estimate.

Stocks are set for a relatively steady start as investors look beyond AI winners, Bloomberg's Michael Msika writes: shares seen as vulnerable to disruption are now outperforming those seen as the technology's biggest beneficiaries. Thursday's decline was concentrated in technology, but the broader market carried on, with the equal-weight S&P 500 finishing up 0.8%, its best day since 2024 relative to the cap-weighted index; advancers outnumbered decliners by about two-to-one and 61% of S&P members are now above their 50-day moving average, the highest in two months.

The AI trade is the culprit once again, but investors do not appear to be turning risk-off so much as repricing the build-out, taking money off the semiconductor trade to reinvest into defensive sectors like staples and utilities. A basket of AI winners is now down 23% from its June highs, while stocks at risk of AI disruption have surged nearly 60% over the same period and now lead for the year.

“Yesterday the market did not stop believing in AI, it simply started asking who pays for it, and at a 5% bond yield that question has an opportunity cost,” said Florian Ielpo, head of macro research at Lombard Odier Asset Management.

“What we’re seeing is a repricing of valuations across the board as rates rise, with neoclouds and other leveraged operators hit hardest,” said Hugh Lam, investment strategist at Betashares in Sydney. “Those financing concerns are weighing on hardware-linked markets like Japan and Korea, which have seen more volatility in recent months.”

The financing angle is the crux: Meta's spending commitments have swelled to $825 billion and its CDS hit a record after results (as we reported), CoreWeave's 5Y CDS blew out to 1,162bps (Bernstein sees a $76 billion funding hole), and credit metrics are flashing their biggest risk-off signal in more than a year. Meanwhile, the S&P Consumer Staples index is up 12% in October, on track for its best month since October 1998, as investors rotate out of tech and into defensives.

Goldman's Rich Privorotsky called Thursday the session that "made the least sense of any day in this selloff", with AI versus the S&P ex-AI suffering its worst relative day since the DeepSeek moment. His summary of the AI capex dilemma: "You either cut capex, delay deployment or increasingly fund through equity. None are particularly supportive of equity prices." The flip side, as he puts it: "Rates: AI loses, bonds win" (a theme his desk laid out earlier this week and McElligott echoed). Goldman Prime notes that all three hedge fund strategy groups lost more than 1% on the same day for the first time since Covid, with multi-strats down 1.9%, the second-worst day since the April 2025 tariff selloff, while TMT specialist Sean Johnstone sums up the mood: "strong AI demand is not enough."

JPMorgan's Market Intel desk says Thursday's Nasdaq selloff showed the fragile sentiment around AI financing, with chatter around a possible US/Israeli strike on Iran after the midterms sparking a broader tech-led de-risking; its cash desk saw long-onlys 3x better for sale while hedge funds were 2.6x better to buy, mostly covering. With MSFT, GOOGL and AMZN reporting next week, investors "may remain low conviction to add risk", though the team stays Tactically Bullish, favoring cyclicals outside tech while selectively buying tech weakness in semis and memory. JPM's Jay Barry notes Thursday's 15-21bp drop in Treasury yields was the largest one-day decline since March 2023, as yields have become increasingly correlated with the Nasdaq.

Elsewhere, SpaceX continued to disrupt the telecom market, aiming to secure at least 80,000 US cell sites and in talks with at least one major infrastructure owner, which is why towers are flying and carriers are getting hit on both sides of the Atlantic. Governments, banks and airlines are still racing to patch critical flaws in PHP, the language underpinning as much as 70% of the internet, which researchers uncovered with the help of AI tools (as we noted yesterday). In politics, President Trump travels to Florida today after rallying in Iowa for GOP Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson, while Goldman desks flag a Democratic sweep at roughly 70% on Polymarket as another AI overhang.

In Europe, the French bond crisis takes a breather: the OAT-Bund spread opened at a fresh high of 176bps, the widest since 2011, before narrowing slightly, but remains set for its biggest weekly widening on record (“Everyone has blown up”). Moody's review of France's rating is due after the close, with a downgrade likely given its negative outlook, and France is deploying the military to back up police ahead of weekend protests. Goldman FICC's take on hedging all of this is here.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is down 0.5% at 634.75, falling for a second day as disappointing earnings, including from Kering's Gucci, add to concerns over the AI trade and elevated oil prices. Telecoms are the worst-performing sector on the SpaceX cell-site report, while energy leads gains alongside construction and real estate. Volvo Car plunged as much as 32% to its lowest since its 2021 listing as cratering China sales and US tariffs hit its turnaround, Kering slid as much as 12%, and Intrum crashed as much as 43% to a record low. Flash PMIs did not help: the euro-area composite fell to 51.9 vs 52.7 expected, dragged down by a surprise plunge into contraction in France (composite 48.4 vs 50.3 est.), while the UK composite jumped to 53.1 vs 51.7 expected. JPM notes semis, luxury, ceasefire and software are among the worst-performing baskets.

  • Electrolux shares gain as much as 12% after the Swedish home-appliance maker’s 3Q EBIT beat expectations by about 5%. Citi says the result comes despite challenging end markets.
  • Sodexo shares rise as much as 6% after the French caterer reported better-than-expected organic sales growth, earnings and dividend for the most recent fiscal year.
  • Munters shares rise as much as 11% after the Swedish heating and air treatment solutions firm reported third-quarter orders that beat the average analyst estimate.
  • Signify shares rise as much as 10% after the light manufacturing company posted results that Morgan Stanley described as a small positive, given relatively low expectations.
  • Kering shares slide as much as 12% after the French luxury-goods company saw further deceleration of third-quarter revenue growth at its key Gucci unit, slower growth in North America as well as persistent weakness in China.
  • Volvo Car shares sink as much as 32% to their lowest since its 2021 listing after what analysts called a weak third quarter, as cratering China sales and US tariffs complicate the automaker’s turnaround.
  • Intrum shares fall as much as 43%, hitting a record low, after the Swedish debt collector reported a goodwill impairment of SEK1.5b due to underperformance in Germany.
  • European Telecom operator shares drop after Bloomberg News reported that SpaceX is in talks to access cell sites in the US, adding to investor concerns around increased competition within the sector.
  • Volvo shares fall as much as 3.5% after the truckmaker’s results were described as a lower-quality beat by analysts.

As storm Austen hits these shores this morning, clouds kept darkening for markets yesterday, as the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once. First, there was mounting stress around France, with the Franco-German 10yr spread (+14.8bps) seeing its biggest daily widening since the initial pandemic turmoil in March 2020. Second, AI fears continued to gather pace, with the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) falling to its lowest level since July, which dragged down equities more broadly. And third, the latest geopolitical fears meant oil prices kept rising as well, with Brent crude (+4.00%) hitting a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl. So collectively, those concerns drove a huge risk-off move, with the 10yr Treasury yield (-16.6bps to 4.95%) seeing its biggest daily decline since August 2024. Although Asian markets are also down, US and European equity futures are relatively flat as I type so the sell-off hasn't accelerated overnight. Today we see global flash PMIs which will as ever be interesting. Note that exactly a month ago today, the US flash numbers were strong and helped drive an almost 15bp increase in both 2yr and 10yr Treasury yields. This felt like a very outsized move relative to the importance this data usually has in the US, but it showed the mood in global bond markets at the time. That couldn’t have been further from the mood in the last 24 hours so an interesting set up for today.

It’s difficult to know where to start given everything going on at the moment, but it was France that led the day’s biggest market moves yesterday. There wasn’t an immediate catalyst for the selloff, but the other two stress points (AI growth fears and higher oil prices) both hit risk appetite, which left France as the most vulnerable given it was already facing market pressure. So all that pushed the Franco-German 10yr spread up to 174bps, taking it to levels last seen at the peak of the sovereign crisis in November 2011. Moreover, the 10yr spread now isn’t too far away from its single-currency-era peak that month, when it closed as high as 189bps.

Those French moves were part of a clear risk-off pattern rather than a global bond selloff, as the 10yr OAT yield (+5.8bps) hit a post-2002 high of 5.07%, whereas the 10yr bund yield (-8.7bps) fell back instead to 3.32%. Moreover, those moves cascaded elsewhere, with the Italian 10yr spread to bunds (+8.7bps) widening to 124bps, the most since the Liberation Day turmoil in April 2025. And the stress was clear from other asset classes, as the STOXX Banks (-4.17%) hit a 4-month low, some -14% off their recent highs in mid-September. The Euro also weakened -0.14% against the US Dollar, while defensive currencies including the yen (+0.87%) and the Swiss France (+0.48%) benefited.

Given the latest stress, yesterday led to fresh questions about whether the ECB would even be able to hike rates again this year. Admittedly, that’s still the baseline market expectation. But with a 69% chance of another hike priced by December this represented a sharp pullback from 90% at the close on Wednesday. So doubts on the sustainability of further ECB hikes are rising. Indeed, the market moves were also creating a broader tightening in financial conditions, with the STOXX 600 down -1.05%, whilst European HY spreads widened +20bps to their highest level since April 2025 at 369bps.

As all that was happening, yesterday also brought a fresh wave of concern around AI-driven growth, reversing some of the optimism from earlier in the week. So it was a rough session for several of the most affected names, and the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) had its worst day since June, whilst CoreWeave’s share price (-10.06%) fell to its lowest since May 2025. That carried over into the CDS space too, where CoreWeave’s 5yr CDS widened +66bps to 1162bps. After its results the night before, Meta (-6.98%) fell and its CDS widened +7.2bps to 118bps. That marked a sharp turnaround from the initially positive after-market reaction to its results on Wednesday night as the sentiment around the company’s rising capex plan soured. Put together, this all helped drive the broader indices lower, with the S&P 500 (-1.21%) posting its worst daily performance since July, whilst the NASDAQ (-2.60%) had its biggest decline since June. However, note that the main defensive sectors rallied strongly, with consumer staples (+3.11%) and utilities (+1.98%) leading the way as two thirds of S&P 500 constituents moved higher, helped by the fall in yields. This also marked the biggest outperformance of the equal-weighted S&P 500 (+0.77%) over the market cap index since July 2024.

The other important theme yesterday was the latest jump in energy prices, driven by mounting fears of a fresh escalation in the Middle East. Indeed, yesterday saw Brent crude (+4.00%) close at a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl, which added to fears about more persistent inflation. Moreover, European natural gas futures (+2.99%) hit another post-2022 high of €90.04/MWh, which particularly hit the continent as growth concerns interacted with the fiscal stress. In part, the latest moves followed a New York Times report we mentioned yesterday, saying that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the midterm elections. So that drove speculation about some kind of escalation after the November 3 vote. And we also heard the Houthis claim a recent attack on Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu oil site, which follows a drone attack at a Saudi oil field the previous day.

In the midst of all these market pressures, an interesting theme was the flight to US Treasuries, which returned to its traditional risk-off role in periods of turmoil. In fact, the 10yr yield fell -16.6bps to 4.95%. Moreover, that came despite some strong US data, demonstrating how the financial stress was weighing on sentiment rather than the fundamentals. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to a 3-month low of 194k in the week ending October 17 (vs. 200k expected). title: Museum Hides Egyptian Mummies For Ridiculous Reason...
desc:
Museum Hides Egyptian Mummies For Ridiculous Reason...

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

A Glasgow museum has pulled Egyptian mummies and other human remains from public view because the long-dead never provided "informed consent" to be displayed.

Yes, really, they've been moved to storage because the 5,000 year old people didn't say it was OK to display their remains.

The decision at Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum follows a draft Human Remains Policy from Glasgow Life, the SNP-funded body that runs the venue, which insists remains should only appear if there is "documented and informed consent from the deceased individual or, in appropriate circumstances, their descendants."

'How absolutely insane.'

GB News' Will Kingston discusses a 'woke madness' debate that has arisen over the removal of mummies on display at a Scottish museum because they cannot give 'informed consent'. https://t.co/LnCYuZTS6V

— GB News (@GBNEWS) October 22, 2026

Visitors found a sign where a painted coffin containing the remains of the priest Nekht once stood: "We have removed human remains from this display as a mark of respect." Also gone are a mummified male head, a mummified right hand recovered from the Valley of the Kings in Luxor, and a mummified right foot.

The artefacts range from roughly 2,000 to 5,000 years old. Glasgow Life says the change "reflects contemporary museum practice" and cites the International Council of Museums' revised Code of Ethics from June 2026, which calls on museums to "uphold the inherent dignity of human remains and promote respect for their significance."

It also references a 2025 All-Party Parliamentary Group on Afrikan Reparations report raising ethical concerns about displaying ancient Egyptian remains.

Of course, the reparations crowd had to be somehow involved.

A Glasgow Life spokesman stated: "In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals."

The organisation is also removing archaeological human remains from the History Discovery Centre and the Scotland's Early People gallery at Kelvingrove, with further removals planned at St Mungo Museum.

What's next? Removing Neanderthals from the Neanderthal museum because they never signed a waiver?

Scottish Conservative MSP Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness at its most ridiculous." He said: "Even Egyptian mummies are now being cancelled by a society so obsessed with modern sensibilities that it has lost all sense of perspective."

"People visit museums to learn about ancient civilisations, not to see history hidden away because it fails to meet today's ideological standards," he added, noting that Glasgow's museums "should be showcasing our history, not quietly removing it to appease the latest trend in political correctness."

Chris McGovern, chairman of the Campaign for Real Education and a former adviser to the Policy Unit at 10 Downing Street, described it as "more virtue-signalling, woke nonsense" and "the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance." He noted: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." He suggested Scottish authorities take their lead from Egyptian museums that "respectfully display human remains."

One visitor, Jonny McFarlane, brought his daughter to the ancient Egypt display after she had been "quite animated" by a book on the subject, only to find the exhibits replaced by the respect sign.

This is not an isolated episode of museums subordinating public education and historical display to contemporary ideological preferences. London institutions have repeatedly altered or obscured exhibits under similar rationales.

In March, London Museum Docklands half-covered a large early 19th-century portrait of Beeston Long, a former Bank of England governor who held investments in Jamaican plantations worked by slave labour, with multicoloured Madras cloth.

The exhibition trail "Caribbean Voices: Shaping Docklands" aimed to "reclaim the histories of colonised Caribbean nations" and celebrate the Windrush Generation's influence.

Information panels stated that artworks which might "obscure" or "sanitise" connections to slavery can "evoke emotional responses" and that museums should give a "voice to those whose cultures have been impacted by colonialism."

Some Caribbean partners reportedly felt "bitter and provoked" or "angry, furious and violated" by the uncovered painting. The cloth, historically exported to the Caribbean, was presented as representing Caribbean nations. A statue of slave trader Robert Milligan had already been removed from outside the museum in 2020 and placed in storage.

In Januar, the Young V&A in Bethnal Green placed books featuring graphic nudity and contested LGBTQ+ material in its children's reading room alongside titles such as The Gruffalo. It Isn't Rude To Be Nude displayed drawings of naked adults with exposed genitalia and captions including "willies aren't silly," with the cover declaring "contains nakedness - and that's OK!"

Another title, Rainbow Revolutionaries, included a glossary defining "gender affirmation surgery," "polyamorous," and "asexual" for young readers.

Parents described the selection as "pornographic," "a useful tool for paedos to groom children," and "psychological warfare." One said an essential part of safeguarding is to alert adults when strangers discuss intimate areas, "never mind actually showing them to kids."

Kate Barker of LGB Alliance called it "grooming in plain sight" and "an egregious safeguarding failure." Shadow equalities secretary Claire Coutinho noted the absurdity of banning children from wearing costumes while allowing material on polyamory and pansexuality. The V&A, chaired by Minouche Shafik and run by Sir Tristram Hunt, said staff had reviewed the books to ensure they were "age appropriate."

In December 2025, Brighton and Hove Museums published a blog post arguing that Santa Claus is "too white" and that his judgment of children as "naughty" or "nice" enforces colonial binaries and assumptions of cultural superiority.

The post suggested challenging the binary, recasting Santa in diverse forms including multiple Santas or "Mother Christmases," and prioritising cultural exchange over judgment.

Toby Young of the Free Speech Union called the museum "po-faced" and asked whether non-Christian countries should leave notes saying "sorry, but this is a decolonised fireplace and white supremacists dressed in red aren't welcome."

Alka Sehgal Cuthbert of Don't Divide Us described the idea as "laughable" and "intellectually vacuous," accusing museums of seeking to "rupture our sense of belonging to a common past and culture." A museum spokesman said the post was intended to prompt reflection and discussion rather than prescribe views.

In April 2024, an LGBTQ audio guide at the Queen's House in Greenwich, produced by a drag performer as part of a "Fierce Queens" event and LGBTQ+ History Month programming, claimed Queen Charlotte, wife of King George III, was "the nation's first royal person of colour" and that "insecure white boys writing history" had omitted this due to "structural racism."

After backlash, the museum later stated the guide was "light-hearted entertainment" by performance artists and "was not 'fact checked'." Critics noted Queen Charlotte was of German ancestry with no evidence of non-European heritage.

Former Royal Navy officer Chris Parry called the material "stupid," said it "degrades and defiles our national reputation for historical scholarship," and described the antics as "profoundly racist," calling for public funding to be removed.

In March 2024, Hastings Museum and Art Gallery, in association with the Hastings Queer History Collective and funded by Arts Council England, claimed that some birds are "queer" because female pheasants supposedly change sex after they stop laying eggs and develop male-coloured feathers.

The pamphlet stated that "queer behaviour in the animal kingdom" had been "ignored or hidden from the public" since the 18th century and that "with queerness visible in the natural world, the argument that it is somehow 'unnatural' begins to unravel."

A fossilised dinosaur footprint was even said to have "queer history" because of the personal life of the boy who found it.

Biologist Dr Emma Hilton stated: "The only vertebrates that change sex are all fish. Birds do not change sex." She noted that older female animals can develop male features due to hormonal changes, "but we would not say that older women had changed sex if they have a bit of a moustache."

In January 2024, Madrid's Prado Museum reviewed thousands of painting descriptions and signs to remove terms such as "dwarf," "deformed," and "disabled" to align with Spanish disability legislation.

Descriptions of Velázquez works were altered, titles such as "Prince Felipe and the Dwarf, Miguel Soplillo" were shortened, and "Portrait of a Dwarf" became "Portrait of a Buffoon." The museum said it was listening to "political consensus" and revisiting signs that "now we find are out of step with the times."

Across these cases, publicly funded institutions have repeatedly prioritised contemporary ideological frameworks over the straightforward presentation of artefacts, art, and evidence.

Critics consistently describe the pattern as the subordination of history and education to political fashion.

Museums exist to show the past as it was, not as current sensitivities require it to appear. When they hide the dead, cover the portraits, rewrite the labels, and invent queer animals, they stop being museums and become something else entirely.

title: "Those Times Are Gone": Volvo Crashes As China Sales Collapse, BofA Recommends Default Protection
desc:
"Those Times Are Gone": Volvo Crashes As China Sales Collapse, BofA Recommends Default Protection

Volvo Cars shares in Stockholm crashed the most since the company's October 2021 listing. The Swedish automaker announced another 2,500 job cuts and warned that its Chinese sales are under severe pressure.

Third-quarter deliveries in China plunged 40% as domestic brands gained ground with cheaper electric vehicles.

"Nobody will be successful with the old recipe where you had global cars developed in Europe and sold them at a premium price" in China, CEO Hakan Samuelsson told analysts on the earnings call earlier today.

Samuelsson emphasized, "Those times are gone." In other words, Volvo is no longer competitive in overseas markets.

The 2,500 job cuts represent about 6% of Volvo's workforce and will primarily affect Sweden. They form part of a turnaround strategy to save an additional 5 billion kronor, following 3,000 job cuts announced last year.

Bank of America analyst Stephanie Vincent recommended buying protection against a default by Volvo Car AB, warning that deteriorating finances and prolonged weakness in China and the U.S. are leaving the Swedish automaker's senior unsecured bonds maturing in 2029 and 2030 at risk.

Vincent added more color:

Spreads not reflecting b/s risks: Buy 5y CDS/UW ‘29s-‘30s

We move our recommendation on VOVCAB 5Y CDS to Buy Protection, from Sell Protection. We maintain our UW recommendation on the VOVCAB' 29-'30s senior unsecured bonds on fundamental deterioration at the company (free cash flow, or CFO less capex, has been negative for three straight quarters and for full-year 2025) and relative value (the bonds still trade tight to BB2-BB1 credits in the ICE BofA BB Euro High Yield Index). Volvo's 3Q and ytd results have been negatively impacted by a significant downturn in China (ytd revenues down 40%) and the U.S. (ytd revenues down 19%). 30th September 2026 cash balances have declined to levels not seen since 2018, while gross debt has remained roughly stable since 2025. Further volatility could be seen if the new management team re-evaluates the medium-term production plans and footprint (Klaus Zelllmer plans to assume the President/CEO position in 3Q27). We are MW on near-term maturities (VOVCAB' 27s/'28s) due to the business' previous market access and overall liquidity.

U.S., China very tough markets for Volvo Car

The U.S. market was hit by current tariffs and the removal of incentives for electrified cars that hit imported EV margins (Volvo Car only produces the EX90 in the U.S. at present, with the XC60 planned to have a SOP in January 2027). The plan for the U.S. market is to localise production for the XC60, and to also bring product offering, marketing and sales closer to its U.S. customers along four regions. There will also be PHEV offerings for the XC90 and XC60 shortly after deliveries start in Europe. In China the market remains very challenged particularly for the Western Premium manufacturers and management notes "the next two years will remain very tough." The production plans are to deliver the first two of six new cars tailored for China, developed in partnership with Geely. Europe is the sole profitable market now, with BEV/battery electric sales reaching 45% share in 3Q (versus 30% in 3Q25), driven by the EX30.

Cash flow a core focus.

Management explicitly highlights that cash is being prioritised. We note that Volvo management believes 4Q26 cash flow will be stronger than 3Q26 due to inventory reductions (however this action could pressure margins due to de-stocking). Overall liquidity is well above management’s view of the minimums needed: the business has cash of SEK 32bn and total liquidity of SEK 55bn. However, the net cash position has deteriorated meaningfully, to a level of SEK 725mn (our estimate, from peak levels of close to SEK 37bn, seen in 4Q21).

LT targets maintained.

Capex, cost actions at forefront. Volvo Car is maintaining its longer-term goal of adjusted EBIT margins >8% and is adding new initiatives: a 30% reduction in capex versus 2024 levels (could lead to lower cash needs of c. SEK 13bn by our estimates) and reinforcing the cost savings. The company is also targets another SEK 5bn in additional cost savings by the end of 2027 (primarily via headcount initiatives).

Volvo shares in Stockholm crashed 30% on Friday morning, marking their worst intraday decline on record.

The selloff reduced Volvo's market value to 29.8 billion kronor ($2.68 billion), about 80% below its 2021 listing valuation.

desc:
"We Should Not Have Done It": Thiel Breaks With Trump Over Iran War, Warns America May Not "Have The Hard Power"

One day after we reported that Donald Trump Jr. has privately broken with his father over the Iran war, Peter Thiel, the PayPal and Palantir (PLTR) co-founder who was the first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016 and the biggest funder of super PACs behind JD Vance's 2022 Senate run, has also drawn a line in the sand over Trump's defining foreign-policy gamble.

In audio from an Oct. 12 private lecture in Nashville obtained by Decoded by POLITICO (Calder McHugh), Thiel told the room:

"I'm skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it. There were a lot of mistakes that were made."

"Maybe we don't have the hard power. Maybe we're going to lose the soft power war."

In other words, one of the architects of the MAGA-tech alliance now thinks the war was a mistake and that America may not be strong enough to finish it. The scoop crossed overnight:

🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Peter Thiel, one of Trump's most influential billionaire backers, says the Iran war was a MISTAKE

"I think we should not have done it. There were a lot of mistakes that were made."

Thiel made the comments last week during a private lecture in Nashville.

He also raised... pic.twitter.com/FkTnpb91sm

— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 22, 2026

Thiel on the Iran war: "I think we should not have done it" https://t.co/0JG5vUcY0r

— Alex Burns (@alexanderburns) October 22, 2026

Below we walk through what Thiel said, the even stranger parts of the lecture, and why it lands at exactly the wrong moment for the White House.

"The Sword Of Damocles"

Per Politico, Thiel spent much of the lecture on what he called the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on Rumsfeld and Cheney, and then said this:

"I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late... And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran."

("Persecute" is the word in Politico's transcript. We assume he meant "prosecute," though at this point in the war, who knows.) Translation: the president's most cerebral backer is publicly speculating that Trump officials face war-crimes exposure. Very reassuring.

Thiel also recounted a meeting with Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after Oct. 7, in which he asked about Israel's plans for Gaza. According to Thiel, Netanyahu replied: "I can't just Dresdenize it," a reference to the Allied firebombing that killed roughly 25,000 people.

Still On Team Trump (Sort Of)

To be fair, Thiel didn't defect. Politico says he "highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president," and framed his critique as opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars rather than to Trump personally. That's the Vance-wing argument, and Politico reported back in March that Vance himself was "skeptical" of striking Iran before the war began. Neither Thiel's representatives nor the White House responded to Politico. Put differently, this is the restrainer wing of the coalition saying in private what it can't say from the podium, and the audio got out 12 days before the Nov. 3 midterms.

title: Europe Went All In On EVs. Now Its Automakers Are Losing Out
desc:
Europe Went All In On EVs. Now Its Automakers Are Losing Out

Authored by Kevin Stocklin via The Epoch Times,

Global sales of electric vehicles (EVs) in 2025 increased by 20 percent over the previous year, exceeding 20 million units worldwide, with much of the increase driven by Europe, where sales jumped by 30 percent, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

But even in a red-hot market, European carmakers are struggling to turn a profit on EVs.

50K LAYOFFS
Volkswagen, Europe's largest electric vehicle maker, announced in September that it would lay off 50,000 workers.

Stellantis, Europe's second-largest auto manufacturer, reported write-downs of 22.2 billion euros ($24.9 billion) as part of its EV "reset" in the second half of 2025, largely due to overinvestment in electric cars.

Operating profit margins at Volkswagen, Europe's largest carmaker, fell to 1.8 percent in 2025 from 5.6 percent in 2024, and the company announced that it would lay off an additional 50,000 workers, amounting to 15 percent of its workforce.

Europe's automakers are caught between two adversaries: Chinese automakers that are aggressively taking market share and undercutting profit margins, and their own governments, which have attempted to force a complete transition to EVs regardless of consumer demand.

In 2023, the European Union mandated a 100 percent elimination of tailpipe carbon dioxide emissions starting in 2035, effectively banning the sale of new internal combustion engine vehicles, though it recently revised that to a 90 percent emissions cut.

In response to these and other mandates, car companies invested in new EV production lines, with Volkswagen alone committing $193 billion in 2023 to electrify its fleet.

"I think that European auto manufacturers are paying the price for paying more attention to what regulators want than what their customers are asking for," Jeff Degner, a research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research, told The Epoch Times.

He calls much of the money spent on the EV transition "government-induced malinvestment."

Volkswagen assembly workers perform final checks and corrections on electric cars in the paint shop at the Volkswagen electric car factory in Emden, Germany, on Feb. 24, 2026. Focke Strangmann/Getty Images

Overestimating Demand, Underestimating China

In announcing this year's write-downs from its EV "reset," Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa concurred.

"The charges announced today largely reflect the cost of overestimating the pace of the energy transition that distanced us from many car buyers' real-world needs, means and desires," Filosa said in a February statement.

America's largest auto manufacturers, Ford and General Motors, have been more cautious about going electric than their European counterparts and have pulled back faster as losses have accumulated.

"The number one trend in the auto industry so far this decade is just the explosive growth in Chinese auto exports."
- Garrett Nelson, equity analyst, Center for Financial Research and Analysis

In January, General Motors announced a $6 billion write-down, shortly after Ford announced a $19.5 billion write-down, as both companies stepped back from their EV commitments.

"EV adoption hasn't developed at the pace or with the economics many of those original commitments assumed, and at the same time, European automakers are facing a much more competitive market," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, told The Epoch Times.

After starting from virtually zero several years ago, Chinese autos made up 20 percent of the EU's battery-electric sales by May 2026, Streaty said.

Chinese automakers have captured the majority of global EV sales, matching Western carmakers in quality and features and beating them on price. Some Chinese models, such as BYD's Seagull, which sells for approximately $10,000 in China, are not only undercutting competitors on price but also delivering on quality, according to reviews by publications such as InsideEVs and Top Gear Philippines.

For European markets, BYD rebranded and upgraded the Seagull as the Dolphin Surf, which launched at a discount price of $22,400 but now sells for about $25,800. This falls under the price of comparable European-made models such as the Citroën ë-C3, which starts at about $26,200, but remains higher than budget models such as the Dacia Spring at $20,100 and the Renault Twingo E-Tech at $21,800.

"The number one trend in the auto industry so far this decade is just the explosive growth in Chinese auto exports," Garrett Nelson, equity analyst at the Center for Financial Research and Analysis, told The Epoch Times. He estimates that China is now exporting more than 1 million vehicles per month.

"They've invested very heavily in infrastructure, in logistics, in order to be able to export so much more than they used to," Nelson said.

China's automobile exports rose by 53 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, while exports of new energy vehicles more than doubled, according to Chinese regime data.

"The European market is really being flooded with low-cost Chinese EVs," Nelson said, and Europe's 10 percent tariffs and other duties on Chinese cars have failed to halt China's expansion.

Vehicles made by Chinese EV manufacturer BYD, at the Port of Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, China, on Feb. 22, 2025. Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images

China's Competitive Advantages

The major Chinese auto brands are BYD, Geely, SAIC, and Changan. In 2025, BYD overtook Tesla as the world's largest seller of EVs.

According to Degner, BYD's production costs are 20 percent to 30 percent lower than those of European carmakers for similar models. But European regulators, even as they pushed domestic auto companies to switch to EVs, simultaneously passed mandates that made manufacturing in Europe significantly more expensive.

This included a state-mandated transition away from coal and other fossil fuels in favor of wind and solar power, resulting in Europeans now paying some of the highest energy and electricity costs in the industrialized world, multiples of those in China.

"The Chinese have a competitive advantage, but that competitive advantage was created because of the high cost that European regulators are imposing," Degner said.

Europeans are now paying some of the highest energy and electricity costs in the industrialized world.

"I would say that the Europeans only have themselves to blame as they have put into place, whether at the national or international level in the EU, the kinds of regulations that are making life more difficult for the [auto] industry as a whole."

In addition, over decades, China has built a global infrastructure for mining and shipping raw materials for batteries, including graphite, lithium, and cobalt. The majority of these materials are also refined, processed, and manufactured into batteries in China.

And Chinese companies benefit from scale and an enormous domestic market.

An employee works on batteries for electric vehicles at the Leap Energy factory, in Huzhou, Zhejiang Province, China, on April 26, 2026. Adek Berry/AFP via Getty Images

Of the 20 million EVs sold worldwide last year, more than 13 million were sold in China, and more than half of worldwide sales were Chinese-made vehicles, according to the IEA.

In addition, a February report by the Rhodium Group states that Chinese automakers benefit from extensive vertical integration of the manufacturing process, as well as state grants, tax incentives, and preferential financing.

Lessons for US Carmakers

Is Europe's EV adventure a cautionary tale for the United States?

The Trump administration believes that it is. The administration eliminated federal tax breaks for EV buyers and canceled the tailpipe emissions and fuel efficiency regulations imposed by the Biden administration that would have effectively phased out many gasoline-powered models.

And there is reason to doubt that most Americans want electric cars.

While EV sales surged in Europe, the United States went in the opposite direction, with electric car sales plummeting by 45 percent in the fourth quarter of 2025 compared with the fourth quarter of 2024. America's annual EV sales in 2025 ended up slightly lower than in 2024, at about 1.5 million vehicles.

EVs remain a niche market in the United States, where driving distances are often longer and the charging infrastructure remains sparse enough to give EV owners "range anxiety" on longer trips. Beyond this, there is the concern that EV demand has been highly dependent on government mandates and subsidies.

According to the IEA, the increase in European sales was partially driven by political mandates, specifically the tightening of the EU carbon dioxide emissions limits that came into effect in 2025, targeting a 15 percent reduction from 2021 levels.

Conversely, the sharp decline in U.S. sales coincided with the Trump administration's cancellation of the $7,500 tax credit for EV purchases.

"Once that expired, the demand went from about 12 percent of the U.S. auto market down to 6 percent within a year, and so I think that is an indicator that the overall consumer taste for EVs is still not where regulators would like to see it," Degner said.

EVs remain a niche market in the United States, where driving distances are often longer.

Having a market so dependent on government incentives creates a significant risk for carmakers when deciding on corporate strategy and potentially hundreds of millions of dollars in capital investments. Even Tesla, which has been selling EVs profitably, reported in July that its operating income fell by 57 percent.

However, outside of the United States, EVs are expanding rapidly throughout North America and South America.

While to date, trade barriers have largely kept Chinese cars out of the United States, America is being encircled, with Chinese carmakers making rapid inroads in Brazil, Mexico, and Canada.

Electric and gas-powered vehicles are parked in a lot at the Tesla factory in Fremont, Calif., on July 26, 2025. Gary Wang/The Epoch Times

BYD began selling EVs in Brazil, South America's largest market, in 2022. By 2025, Chinese carmakers produced 85 percent of EVs sold in Brazil, according to an IEA report.

Recent trade deals among China and Mexico and Canada have opened those markets to Chinese carmakers, and sales of Chinese cars surged in Mexico last year, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

"This is very concerning for U.S. automakers," Nelson said. "You're seeing trade groups raise red flags and sound the alarm regarding what this might mean."

Finding Ways to Compete

Could U.S. automakers compete in the EV market if they wanted to? Some analysts say yes, with conditions.

"In the U.S. market, in light of rising gas prices right now, we're seeing a decline in EV demand, but a significant increase in the demand for hybrid engines, which do have, of course, some electronic and battery components," Degner said.

"By cutting red tape and access to those kinds of technologies, and certainly those kinds of natural resources, there's ample evidence that the U.S. could compete with BYD if those barriers were removed."

America could match China's access to essential raw materials, but mining prohibitions and other regulations have held up this development, Degner said.

A plug-in hybrid vehicle in Irvine, Calif., on Nov. 28, 2023. A plug-in hybrid drives like a fully electric car for short trips, but operates like a gasoline or hybrid vehicle for long-distance travel. John Fredricks/The Epoch Times

Japanese automakers Toyota, Honda, and Nissan have largely sidestepped the battery-electric vehicle market, focusing instead on hybrids, in addition to traditional gasoline-powered cars.

title: US Blacklists Sam Altman's Old Y Combinator China Pick Over Startup Built On Stolen Google AI Secrets
desc:
US Blacklists Sam Altman's Old Y Combinator China Pick Over Startup Built On Stolen Google AI Secrets

Of all the people who could end up on a US sanctions list for bankrolling stolen Google AI technology, a former Microsoft executive hand-picked by Sam Altman to run Y Combinator's China arm was probably not on many bingo cards. And yet here we are.

On Monday, the State Department blacklisted Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, the AI startup founded by convicted ex-Google engineer Linwei Ding, along with MiraclePlus, the Chinese venture firm founded by ex-Microsoft AI scientist Lu Qi, and three MiraclePlus-managed funds, for providing seed financing to Zhisuan. According to Bloomberg, the measures may include freezing US assets and banking restrictions.

The best part of the story is Lu's resume, which reads like a tour of every major tech power center of the past 20 years: the stuff corporate espionage movie scripts are made of. Per Bloomberg:

Lu, a former Microsoft executive, was recruited in 2017 by Baidu Inc. to oversee the Chinese search leader's AI efforts, only to quit a year later citing personal reasons. In 2018, Lu – recruited by then-Y Combinator President Sam Altman – joined the US firm to help create YC China.

When Y Combinator abandoned the expansion a year later, Lu and his team simply kept going under the MiraclePlus brand. That's the same MiraclePlus that, according to the State Department, gave a Chinese startup seed money in exchange for equity after its founder showed up touting his inside knowledge of Google's AI infrastructure.

"An Important Missing Piece Of Our Puzzle"

Some quick background on Lu Qi (who also goes by Qi Lu, depending on which side of the Pacific is writing the press release). After rising to executive vice president of engineering at Yahoo, Lu was personally recruited by Steve Ballmer to Microsoft, where he ran Bing, Office and Skype and later helped shape Satya Nadella's AI and bots strategy. In January 2017, Baidu poached him as group president and COO to run its AI push. He lasted 16 months, leaving in May 2018 for "personal and family reasons" and which, as CNBC reported at the time, really meant he just wanted to spend more time in the US.

Three months later he had a new job. In August 2018, Altman's Y Combinator announced Lu would lead YC China (as well as YC's research arm and a new research center in Seattle), with Altman (who just like Ballmer, personally recruited Lu) calling China "an important missing piece of our puzzle."

Well, the puzzle didn't stay assembled for long. In November 2019, in the middle of the trade war, YC pulled the plug on China. Lu spun the team out as MiraclePlus (Qiji Chuangtan in Chinese), which has since become one of China's busiest early-stage investors: it writes $300K checks for 7% stakes and runs two cohorts a year. Its portfolio includes some of China's hottest AI names, among them AI inference platform SiliconFlow and robotics maker AgiBot, both of which are considering Hong Kong listings (and both of which now have a sanctioned backer, which is probably not the line the bankers wanted in the prospectus).

"Replicate Google's Technology... To Fit China's National Conditions"

So how did a Beijing incubator end up on the same list as the guy who walked out of Google with its AI supercomputer blueprints?

According to the State Department fact sheet, Ding applied to MiraclePlus's incubation program on behalf of Zhisuan, "touting his experience with and knowledge of Google's technology and internal systems" and claiming Zhisuan could replicate Google's "super intelligence" infrastructure technology. State says Ding used the program to pitch his ability to replicate Google's technology to fit China's national conditions, and that "MiraclePlus gave seed capital in exchange for an ownership stake in Zhisuan."

That pitch will sound familiar to regular readers. When we first covered Ding's arrest back in March 2024, the indictment quoted a WeChat promo for his Shanghai startup, in which he bragged:

"We have experience with Google's ten-thousand-card computational power platform; we just need to replicate and upgrade it—and then further develop a computational power platform suited to China's national conditions."

In other words, the business plan was the stolen goods. You'd think a seasoned VC might have asked one or two follow-up questions about where the "experience" came from.

MiraclePlus, for its part, denies investing in Zhisuan at all. In a statement on Tuesday, the firm said the sanctions were imposed without any prior communication, and that it is in talks with relevant parties to have them lifted and expects the matter to be resolved through "candid communication." Which, coming from a firm called MiraclePlus, may take a miracle of its own.

The penalties were imposed under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (PAIPA), signed into law in January 2023 to go after foreign beneficiaries of US trade-secret theft. In addition to Zhisuan and MiraclePlus (formally Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management), the list includes MiraclePlus's Phase I and Phase II venture funds and an entity wholly owned by Phase I. Put differently, Washington went after the money too.

Apple Notes, A Borrowed Badge And A One-Way Ticket

As for the man, the Ding saga has been a long one. Between May 2022 and April 2023, the Google software engineer uploaded more than 2,000 pages of confidential AI trade secrets to his personal Google Cloud account, covering the architecture of Google's custom TPU chips, its GPU systems, the software that orchestrates thousands of chips into a supercomputer, and a custom SmartNIC used for high-speed networking. In other words, the crown jewels of Google's AI stack.

The method was low-tech to the point of comedy: Ding copied the data into the Apple Notes app on his Google-issued MacBook, converted it to PDFs and uploaded those. He also had a colleague scan his access badge so it looked like he was working from Google's US office while he was actually in China. He secretly affiliated himself with two China-based AI companies while still on Google's payroll, applied to a Shanghai government "talent plan" promising to help China build "computing power infrastructure capabilities that are on par with the international level," and downloaded more files less than two weeks before resigning in December 2023. Then he booked a one-way ticket to Beijing.

When the charges first dropped, we couldn't resist pointing out the obvious problem with stealing from Google in the Gemini era:

An ex-Google engineer was charged with stealing artificial intelligence technology while secretly working with two companies based in China. So China's AI is now racist, woke and wrong about everything

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) March 6, 2024

The case later became Exhibit A in what Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang called China's "open secret" tech-theft operation (Jun 14, 2025), in which Wang argued that China is on par with the US on algorithms "because of large-scale espionage."

Fourteen Convictions, One Year

On January 29, a San Francisco jury convicted Ding on seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of trade secret theft, which on paper carried a maximum of 15 years and 10 years per count, respectively. Then the case started to deflate.

In August, Judge Vince Chhabria tossed all seven espionage convictions, ruling there was insufficient evidence Ding intended to benefit the Chinese government (as opposed to just Chinese companies, which apparently is a different thing). And on September 1, he was sentenced to 12 months minus one day, plus two years of supervised release, about $198,000 in restitution to Google and a $2,500 fine. Prosecutors had asked for 70 months; the defense wanted three months of home confinement.

"The idea of a non-custodial sentence is very hard to swallow for me," Chhabria said, which tells you how close Ding came to serving his time from the couch. For context, $198,000 in restitution for the blueprints of Google's TPU stack, which is precisely what anyone trying to build an AI supercomputer without access to Nvidia's best chips would want, is what one might call a bargain.

Which is probably why Washington is now going after the money instead. If the courts won't make the penalty sting for the engineer, the State Department can at least make it sting for whoever funded him.

Beijing, naturally, is not amused. On Tuesday China's commerce ministry expressed "firm opposition" to the sanctions, urged the US to "correct its erroneous practice," and threatened unspecified "necessary measures." The ministry also insisted China's AI achievements are the result of long-term basic research and open cooperation, and have "nothing to do with the so-called 'stealing of trade secrets.'" Sure.

Altman's China Problem, Then And Now

None of this is Altman's fault, of course: he hired a Microsoft and Baidu veteran with a sterling resume in 2018, and YC exited China a year later. MiraclePlus's alleged Zhisuan deal came four years after that. Still, the irony is hard to miss.

The same Altman who once called China the "missing piece" of YC's puzzle spent last month lining up with Dario Amodei and Elon Musk to ask Washington for embedded evaluators, an antitrust waiver and a talk with Beijing, while China goes full send, as we discussed in "'Pace The Frontier': Amodei, Altman & Musk Team Up Against The AI Singularity While China Goes Full Send". Meanwhile, OpenAI is busy defending itself against Apple's lawsuit alleging that OpenAI misused Apple's hardware trade secrets after hiring its former VP of iPhone and Apple Watch product design. Trade secrets, it seems, are having a moment.

The Real Penalty Lands On The Cap Table

The sanctions themselves are probably more symbolic than crippling. MiraclePlus is a Beijing-based firm investing in Chinese startups, and its exposure to the US banking system is likely limited. But the signal matters: for the first time in this case, Washington is targeting the capital behind the theft as well as the thief, and it is doing so with a law built for exactly that purpose.

The more interesting question is what happens next to the MiraclePlus portfolio. SiliconFlow and AgiBot are both eyeing Hong Kong IPOs, and global investors tend to get nervous when a company's early backer is on a US sanctions list, regardless of what the backer says about "candid communication." We suspect the lawyers for those deals are having a busy week.

As for Ding, a jury found he stole Google's AI crown jewels, a judge gave him a year, and his alleged backers got blacklisted. Something tells us the next would-be Ding will look at that math and decide the risk-reward is still pretty attractive.

title: "The State Does Not Create Wealth; It Consumes It": Europe's Socialist Model Hits The Wall
desc:
"The State Does Not Create Wealth; It Consumes It": Europe's Socialist Model Hits The Wall

Authored by Daniel Lacalle via dlacalle.com,

Decades of bloated government, entitlements, subsidies, and mass migration have destroyed Europe's competitiveness and growth, all paid for with ever-rising taxes and more debt. They have also created enormous social discontent. Taxpayers are exhausted, and the recipients of subsidies are looting and vandalizing the streets. The flames in French cities are the bill that is arriving.

On Saturday 17 October, France burned again. What began as marches against the cost of living and the state of public schools turned into the worst violence the country has seen in decades. According to the French government, 550,000 people took to the streets, 1,200 were arrested, and 150 police officers were injured. In Limoges, rioters set the city hall ablaze; in Marseille, they broke into the city hall; and in Lyon, they torched the tourist office. AFP reporters on the ground described scenes more intense than the 2023 riots and the Yellow Vest protests of 2018 and 2019, six months before a presidential election. Major cities, including Paris, Marseille, and Lille, suffered enormous commercial damage with smashed shopfronts, shattered glass, and ransacked retail spaces. In Bordeaux, Mayor Thomas Cazenave reported that up to 100 stores were looted in his city alone.

The riot images will be explained away as the work of a violent fringe, and it will be said that the mob that loots luxury boutiques and supermarkets certainly does not represent the hundreds of thousands who marched peacefully. However, the anger is real, and it has a cause.

Europe has spent half a century building the largest welfare state in the world on the promise that government could guarantee prosperity, security, and equality for everyone. That model has completely failed, and the people who were promised everything are discovering that the state only delivers stagnation and impoverishment.

France is the clearest example of what "democratic socialism" does to a rich nation. France is the most state-heavy economy in the European Union. French public spending reached 57.2% of GDP in 2025, the second highest in the EU and 7.7 points above the average. Its tax burden is among the highest in the world, at 45.3% of GDP in 2024, behind only Denmark in the EU. Public debt rose to 119% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, and the deficit stood at 5.1% of GDP in 2025. If big government, high taxes, and immigration delivered prosperity and social peace, France would be paradise. Instead, the protesters on the streets of Paris are demanding more of the same medicine that made them sick.

The welfare machine eats the economy.

France is not an extreme or single example. The disease is continental. Government expenditure in the European Union reached 49.5% of GDP in 2025 and 49.8% in the euro area. Half of the economy is directly controlled by the state, and much of the rest is regulated, subsidized, or taxed to the point of exhaustion. Social protection benefits alone reached 4,925 billion euros in 2024, 27.3% of the EU's GDP, after growing 6.9% in a single year while nominal GDP grew only 4.4%.

Add the subsidies. European governments spent 340 billion euros on energy subsidies in 2024 and another 168 billion euros in state aid. Governments first make energy expensive with taxes, regulations, and ideological mandates, then subsidize the very costs they created, and finally borrow to pay for the subsidies. Citizens pay three times, as consumers, as taxpayers, and as the future holders of the debt.

The debt is the inevitable consequence. Greece ended 2025 with public debt at 146.1% of GDP, Italy at 137.1%, France at 115.6%, Belgium at 107.9%, and Spain at 100.7%. And those figures hide the largest liability of all. According to Eurostat, the pension entitlements already accrued in social insurance schemes reach 500% of GDP in Spain, 462% in Austria, 438% in Italy, 397% in France, and 347% in Germany, almost all of them unfunded, according to Eurostat. These are promises that no government can keep without crushing the next generation with taxes or destroying the purchasing power of the currency.

Germany, once the engine of Europe, now transfers 127.4 billion euros from the federal budget to its pension system in 2026, rising to 132 billion in 2027. Spain's Social Security debt has almost quadrupled since 2018, from 34,888 million to 136,176 million euros, and social contributions cover pension payments only until early October. The welfare state now lives on borrowing against the future rather than on what the economy produces.

Competitiveness destroyed

There is no free lunch. Every euro of spending must be paid for by the productive economy, and Europe's productive economy is suffocating. The International Monetary Fund expects the euro area to grow just 1.1% in 2026, compared with 2.3% in the United States, with France at a miserable 0.4% and Italy at 0.8%. Labor productivity per hour worked in the EU stood at only 78.5% of the US level in 2024, and in 2025 it grew just 0.4% compared with 1.6% in the United States.

German industrial production has fallen every year since 2022, and the BDI industry association no longer expects a recovery in 2026, only stagnation. Output in energy-intensive sectors is at its lowest level since the end of 2023. That is what happens when energy is made artificially expensive, labor is taxed at confiscatory rates, regulation multiplies, and capital flees.

Inflation makes the situation even worse. Euro area inflation rose to 3.8% in September 2026, with energy prices up 18.9% year-on-year. Governments that printed and borrowed their way through every crisis now discover that the real wages of their citizens cannot keep up. The cost-of-living crisis that sent hundreds of thousands into French streets has its roots in decades of too much government, not too little.

Mass migration worsens the situation.

Instead of reforming, European governments chose to import the illusion of growth. On January 2025, 46.7 million people living in the EU had been born outside it, 10.4% of the population, and the number of non-EU citizens rose by 1.6 million in a single year to 30.6 million. Immigration may be a powerful engine of prosperity when it is carefully selected for skills and enters flexible labor markets with low taxes and limited welfare. Europe did the opposite. It combined mass migration with rigid labor markets, enormous taxes, and the most excessive welfare benefits on the planet.

The result was predictable. Many immigrants have no incentive to adapt or participate and are trapped in low-wage jobs and welfare dependency. Thus, public services were stretched beyond capacity, housing became unaffordable in the major cities, and integration failed in entire neighborhoods. Governments used headline GDP inflated by population growth to hide stagnant income per person, while workers saw their wages fall in real net terms as inflation and their taxes rise. This is the evidence of a model that promised everything to everyone and delivered disappointment to all.

When you create a state big enough to promise everything, it delivers almost nothing but takes away everything it can.

Angry taxpayers, entitled mobs

Democratic socialism created two angry Europeans. The first is the angry taxpayer, the middle-class worker, the small business owner, and the self-employed professional who pays more every year and receives worse services, longer waiting lists, unaffordable housing, security problems, and a pension system that will not be there when they retire. The second is entitled Europe, a constituency that has been taught for decades that the state owes it everything and responds to inevitable disappointment with rage and violence.

Both are victims of the same lie. Politicians promised that they could raise taxes on the rich, borrow without limit, and expand entitlements forever with no consequences. They told voters that someone else would pay. Now that someone else, the productive economy, is exhausted. Capital is leaving, young talent is emigrating, industry is closing, and the bill is landing on the middle class and on young people who will inherit the debt.

What Europe needs is less state. Another subsidy, another tax on «the rich» or another emergency fund financed with joint debt will only deepen the crisis. The way forward is to cut unproductive spending, reduce the tax burden on labor and investment, end the subsidy culture that keeps the economy zombified, liberalize markets, and abandon the ideological mandates that have made European industry uncompetitive.

Europe needs a migration policy designed for prosperity rather than electoral calculation, selective, linked to employment, and not to welfare entitlement. It needs a gradual transition from unfunded pay-as-you-go pensions to capitalized systems in which workers own their savings, as Sweden and the Netherlands have shown is possible.

Citizens need to realize the truth, which is that the state does not create wealth; it consumes it.

The riots in France are a warning to America. When a society is told for decades that it is entitled to everything and then discovers that the state is broke, the result is not solidarity but violence.

Democratic socialism promised Europe equality and security. It delivered stagnation, inflation, debt, and rage. If America adopts this system, it will follow the same path of misery and desperation. The sooner Europe abandons democratic socialism, the sooner it can recover the prosperity that made it the envy of the world.

title: Barclays To Axe 5,000 Jobs As Britain's Youth Employment Crisis Deepens
desc:
Barclays To Axe 5,000 Jobs As Britain's Youth Employment Crisis Deepens

Bloomberg cites a Barclays corporate presentation saying the bank is cutting 5,000 jobs as it pushes ahead with cost-cutting measures and adopts artificial intelligence to improve efficiency.

The reductions would affect about 5% of the bank's workforce. The London-based lender employed about 93,000 people globally at the end of 2025, according to Bloomberg data.

Barclays said it was "structurally reducing" costs to "generate capacity for investment." The presentation also touched on organizational simplification and greater efficiency, supported by AI.

Separately, a Bloomberg report says that technology and finance jobs for young people in the UK have fallen sharply.

Payroll jobs for young people in information and communication have plummeted 30% between the end of 2022 and the end of 2025, according to Boston Consulting Group data. Finance jobs for the same age group fell 10%. Combined, the two sectors - that is, about a decline of 45,000 jobs - left about 163,000 employed.

Young folks "are being squeezed out of some of the UK's most important sectors," said Raoul Ruparel, senior director at BCG's Center for Growth, as companies grow more reluctant to hire young workers.
